g1011.g: consider, determined, plan, planned, planning, plotted
g1011.sum: The Greek verb bouleúō means to think a matter through and come to a decision: to consider, deliberate, plan, or resolve. A person may do it alone, as when a king sits down to weigh his chances in war, or with others, as when a council works out what to do. The word carries no moral color of its own. Whether a plan is wise or wicked depends on who is planning and what they intend.

g1063.g: After, and, Because, because, But, doubt, even, For, for, indeed, Let, Now, since, then, to, What, When, Why, yet
g1063.sum: Gár is the Greek word behind most of the "for" statements in the New Testament. It gives the reason behind what was just said. An angel names a child, and gár tells us why. Paul makes a claim, and gár brings the support. A Gospel writer pauses the story, and gár supplies the background a reader needs. Less often it adds force to a reply or a question, as in "No indeed!" or "Why, what evil has He done?" Noticing gár…

g1106.g: advice, consent, decided, judgment, mind, purpose
g1106.sum: Gnṓmē is a Greek word for a mind that has reached a decision. It names a settled conclusion: a considered opinion, a piece of advice, a firm intention, or an agreement shared by more than one person. The NKJV translates it with several words ("decided," "judgment," "advice," "consent," "mind," "purpose") because the word follows whoever has reached the conclusion. That may be a traveling apostle choosing a safer…

g1161.sum: Dé is one of the most frequent connecting words in the Greek New Testament. Its job is to move the reader from one statement to the next. Sometimes it simply carries the story or argument forward, and the NKJV renders it "and," "now," "then," or "so." Other times it turns the reader toward a different subject or a contrasting idea, and the NKJV renders it "but," "yet," or "however." The word itself does not say…

g1271.sum: Diánoia is the Greek word for the mind as the part of a person that thinks things through. It covers reasoning, understanding, and the settled outlook that grows from them. In the NKJV it is usually translated "mind," and sometimes "understanding" or "imagination." The word itself is morally neutral. It names a human faculty, and that faculty can be proud and darkened, or enlightened and devoted to God.

g1437.g: As, But, even, If, if, or, say, that, Though, though, what, Whatever, whatever, when, whenever, Wherever, wherever, whether, Whoever, whoever, whom, whomever
g1437.sum: Eán is one of the main Greek words the New Testament uses for "if." It usually introduces a situation that could really happen, or one that keeps happening in ordinary life. It does not usually picture something everyone knows is untrue. The "if" clause sets the condition, and the rest of the sentence says what follows: "If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us." When eán joins words like "who,"…

g1438.g: another, he, her, herself, Him, him, Himself, himself, His, his, itself, mother, oneself, other, ourselves, own, She, the, their, them, themselves, they, together, you, yourself, yourselves
g1438.sum: Heautoû is the Greek New Testament's ordinary reflexive pronoun. It points an action or a possession back to the person who is doing it. When Jesus warns that "whoever exalts himself will be humbled," heautoû marks the man who lifts himself up. When Paul says Christ "humbled Himself," the same word shows that the Son was the one who chose the lowering. In the plural it can describe a group acting within its own…

g1473.g: became, become, came, come, I, Me, me, Mine, mine, My, my, myself, name, Our, our, ours, ourselves, same, some, time, Us, us, We, we
g1473.w: I, Me, My, We, Us, Our
g1473.sum: Egṓ is the Greek first-person pronoun. It is the word a speaker uses for himself ("I," "me," "my") and, in its plural forms, for a group that includes the speaker ("we," "us," "our"). Most of its uses are ordinary. It marks who receives an action, as in the leper's plea, "You can make me clean" (Mark 1:40), or whose something is, as in " Our Father in heaven" (Matthew 6:9).

g1519.sum: Eis is a Greek preposition that points toward a goal. Most often it marks where someone is going, as when the wise men "had come into the house" (Matthew 2:11). The same forward-pointing sense carries over into other areas. Eis can name the purpose an action serves, the new state or relationship a person enters, or the point in time something reaches. That is why the NKJV renders it in many ways: "to," "into," "in,"…

g1537.g: abundantly, again, among, an, and, appear, are, at, because, between, beyond, By, by, earthly, for, From, from, gave, highly, in, individually, long, Of, of, on, opposite, over, Since, through, throughout, to, which, with, without
g1537.sum: The Greek preposition ek points to where something comes from. Its basic sense is "out of" or "out from." It can describe a voice coming from heaven, a person singled out of a group, a life born of God, or a right standing that rests on faith rather than on works. English translations render it many ways, most often "of," "from," and "by." Behind each of these renderings is the same question: what is this coming out…

g1565.g: He, he, Him, him, His, his, one, other, Peter, same, She, she, that, The, the, their, theirs, them, they, this, those, very
g1565.sum: Ekeînos is the Greek word for "that" or "those." It points at a particular person, time, place, or thing and sets it apart from what lies closer at hand. Sometimes it modifies a noun, as in "that day" or "those days." Often it stands alone as "that one," and the NKJV then renders it "He," "She," or "they." It also fixes events to a precise moment, which the NKJV can render "the same day" or "that very hour." The…

g1722.sum: The Greek preposition en most often places something inside a setting. That setting can be a town, a crowd, a stretch of time, a condition of heart, or a person. From that basic sense it also names the means by which something is done, which is why the NKJV renders it "in," "among," "at," "on," "by," "with," "while," and more. Context, not the English word, shows which relationship is meant. En matters most when…

g1909.sum: Epí is one of the New Testament's busiest prepositions. It links an action or a person to something it rests on, moves toward, presses against, or rules over. A lamp is set on a lampstand. The Holy Spirit comes upon Mary. Children rise against their parents. A faithful servant is made ruler over many things. Epí can also name the ground an action stands on, as when Peter lets down his nets "at Your word." Because…

g2193.g: as, before, even, long, right, Till, till, To, to, Until, until, While, while
g2193.sum: Héōs is the Greek word that marks a limit. It tells the reader how far something goes, whether in time ("until," "till"), in space ("to the end of the earth"), or across a stretch of time during which something must happen ("while it is day"). Joined with a question word, it becomes the cry "How long?" Paying attention to héōs helps readers see where a statement begins and ends. It shows how long a command applies,…

g2198.g: alive, life, lifetime, live, lived, lives, living
g2198.sum: The Greek verb záō means "to live" or "to be alive." It can describe ordinary physical life, such as a sick boy who recovers when Jesus says, "Your son lives" (John 4:50). It can also describe how a person conducts that life, and for whom. In the New Testament, though, the word reaches higher than biology. God is "the living God," the One "who lives forever and ever." The risen Jesus is the One who "was dead, and…

g2222.sum: The Greek word zōḗ means "life": the state of being alive, and sometimes the span of a person's earthly days. The New Testament seldom leaves it at that. Most of its uses describe the life that belongs to God Himself, which He gives to those who belong to His Son. It appears in Jesus' call to "enter into life," in John's frequent phrase "eternal life," and in Paul's contrast between the reign of death and the reign…

g2249.sum: Hēmeîs is the Greek word for "we" when it stands as the subject of a sentence. Greek verbs already show who is acting, so a writer could say "we preach" without adding a separate word for "we." When hēmeîs does appear, the writer has usually chosen to put the group itself in the spotlight. Most often he is setting "us" against someone else, as when the Pharisees tell the healed man, "You are His disciple, but we are…

g235.g: also, and, But, but, contrary, Even, fact, However, however, Indeed, indeed, Moreover, Nevertheless, nevertheless, No, no, only, Rather, rather, than, Therefore, therefore, what, Yes, yes, Yet, yet
g235.w: But, On The Contrary, Nevertheless, Yes
g235.sum: Allá is the New Testament's strong "but." It usually sets aside one idea and puts another in its place. Most often it follows a negative: "not this, but that." When Jesus says, "I did not come to destroy but to fulfill" (Matthew 5:17), the word clears away a false idea and names the true one. Allá can also press a statement forward despite an obstacle, which the NKJV often renders "nevertheless" or "yet." Less often…

g2374.sum: Thýra is the ordinary Greek word for a door: the movable barrier that lets people into a house, an inner room, a prison, a tomb, or the temple, or keeps them out. Because a door can be opened or shut, the New Testament uses it to talk about access, boundaries, and timing. Crowds press around the door of a house in Capernaum, prison doors swing open at night, and a stone is rolled against the door of Jesus' tomb.

g2443.g: by, if, lest, than, That, that, things, this, to
g2443.sum: Hína is one of the most frequent connecting words in the New Testament. It usually introduces a goal and answers the question "why?" When John writes that God gave His Son " that whoever believes in Him should not perish" (John 3:16), hína names what God's giving was meant to achieve. The word also has other jobs. After verbs of praying, asking, or commanding, it often supplies the content of the request or command…

g2532.sum: Kaí is the Greek conjunction usually translated "and." It is the thread that holds New Testament sentences together. Most often it simply joins words and clauses or moves a story forward, which is why NKJV readers meet it as "and," "then," or "now." The same word can also reach forward to a single word and mean "also," include someone in what has just been said, or mean "even" to mark a surprising case. In Paul's…

g2584.sum: Capernaum was a fishing town on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. When Jesus left Nazareth, He made it the home base of His Galilean ministry. The name comes from the Hebrew Kefar Nahum , "village of Nahum." Because the personal name Nahum is connected with comfort or compassion, the name is sometimes rendered "village of comfort." Scripture never explains the name, and it never tells us who this Nahum…

g2596.sum: Katá is a Greek preposition that helps the New Testament say two very different things. Most often it names the standard something follows, as when Paul says that "Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures" (1 Corinthians 15:3). It can also mark opposition: "He who is not with Me is against Me" (Matthew 12:30). Which meaning applies depends on the grammatical form of the word that follows it.

g2839.sum: Koinós is a Greek adjective meaning "common." The New Testament uses it in two ways that pull in opposite directions. In one, "common" means shared , something that belongs equally to everyone in a group. The first believers "had all things in common" (Acts 2:44), Paul calls Titus "a true son in our common faith" (Titus 1:4), and Jude writes of "our common salvation" (Jude 3). In the other, "common" means ordinary…

g288.sum: Ámpelos is the ordinary Greek word for a vine, almost always the grapevine that covered the hillsides of Israel and supplied its wine. Jesus uses it at the Last Supper when He calls the cup "the fruit of the vine." He uses it in the Upper Room when He says, "I am the true vine." James uses it to make a point about honest speech, and Revelation uses it for the harvest of God's judgment.

g2897.sum: Kraipálē is the Greek word behind "carousing" in Luke 21:34, and it appears nowhere else in the New Testament. In ordinary Greek it described heavy drinking and its aftermath: the dizzy, staggering, dull-headed condition we call a hangover. The word covers both the binge and the stupor that follows.

g3165.g: became, came, come, I, Me, me, My, name, some, time
g3165.sum: Mé is the ordinary Greek word for "me" when the speaker receives an action. It most often marks the person being loved, denied, followed, or welcomed. It can also mark the person someone comes toward, or the person who is the subject of an infinitive ("to do," "to be"). In English it usually appears as "me," or as "Me" when Jesus or God is speaking. Sometimes Greek grammar requires an English "I" instead, as in…

g3305.sum: Méntoi is a Greek word of contrast. It sets what actually happened beside what we would have expected, or sets a firm truth against a troubling situation. The NKJV usually renders it "yet," "however," or "nevertheless." Five of its eight New Testament uses are in John's Gospel. There it often marks a moment of hesitation: disciples who wonder but stay silent, rulers who believe but will not confess, and a disciple…

g3326.g: After, after, Afterward, afterward, against, among, and, behind, boldly, follow, followed, from, in, joyfully, later, on, setting, to, when, With, with, without
g3326.sum: Metá is one of the Greek New Testament's most frequent prepositions. It does two main jobs. It can place people or things together, "with," or it can place events in order, "after." The form of the following noun usually tells the reader which job it is doing. As "with," it describes companionship, shared experience, the attitude that accompanies an action, and even conflict when the verb is about fighting. As…

g3387.sum: Mḗtis is a Greek question word that tells you how the speaker expects the question to be answered. It combines a negative with "anyone" or "anything," so it asks, in effect, "No one has done this, have they?" English translations usually render it with a plain "anyone," "any," or "Did," which can make the question sound neutral. In all four New Testament uses, the speaker leans toward "No." Sometimes that "No" is…

g3398.g: least, Less, little, short, small, smaller
g3398.sum: Mikrós is the ordinary Greek word for "small" or "little." It can describe the size of a seed, the height of a man, a short stretch of time, or a person's low standing. The NKJV usually renders it "little," "least," or "small." It is a plain, everyday word, but Jesus and the apostles use it at some of the most revealing moments in the New Testament.

g3403.sum: Mimnḗskō means to remember, to call something to mind, or to be mindful of someone. It appears only four times in the New Testament, and in each one memory does something. A worshiper remembers a wronged brother and leaves his gift at the altar. God is mindful of frail humanity, and Hebrews moves directly to Jesus tasting death for everyone. Believers are told to remember prisoners as if chained with them, and to…

g3415.sum: Mnáomai means "to remember," "to recall," or "to be mindful of." In the New Testament it describes people bringing a past word or event back to mind. Peter remembers Jesus' warning after his denials. The disciples remember His words after the resurrection. A dying thief asks Jesus to remember him. Again and again, remembering in these passages leads somewhere: to tears, to faith, to steadfastness, or to regret.

g3421.g: mention, mind, Remember, remember, remembered, remembering, remembers
g3421.w: Remember, Call To Mind, Make Mention
g3421.sum: Mnēmoneúō is a common New Testament verb meaning "to remember." Scripture rarely uses it for idle recollection. Most often it describes calling something to mind so that it changes what a person believes, feels, or does right now. Jesus asks His anxious disciples, "Do you not remember?" about the loaves (Mark 8:18). He tells them to remember His warnings so that persecution will not catch them off guard (John 16:4).…

g3427.g: came, come, I, Me, me, Mine, My, my, same, some
g3427.sum: When the Greek New Testament says "to me" or "for me" without special stress, it usually uses moí . The word is the ordinary first-person pronoun in the form Greek uses for the person who receives something, benefits from something, or is affected by it. The NKJV usually renders it "me" or "to me." It also appears where English needs "I" or "my," because Greek often expresses ownership as "something is to me."…

g3450.g: become, I, Me, me, Mine, mine, My, my
g3450.sum: Moû is the Greek pronoun most often behind the "my" in the New Testament. It names what belongs to the speaker or is bound to the speaker: "My beloved Son," "these sayings of Mine," "My brethren." Greek grammar also calls for this same form after certain prepositions and verbs, and in comparisons, so English sometimes renders it "Me" or "I" instead. Noticing it helps readers hear who is claiming whom. When the…

g3483.sum: Naí is the New Testament's word for "yes." Most often it answers a question, as when Peter tells the risen Jesus, "Yes, Lord; You know that I love You." It also does more. A speaker can use it to drive home a point, to answer his own question in an argument, or to give solemn agreement to what God has said or done. In the NKJV the same word appears as "Yes," "Even so," and "Surely." In Jesus' teaching and in Paul's…

g3563.sum: The Greek word noûs means "mind" or "understanding." It is the part of a person that thinks, judges, weighs, and decides what is true and what matters. In the New Testament the mind is never a neutral calculator. Paul describes the mind of people who turned from God as "debased" and walking "in the futility of their mind," while believers are called to "be transformed by the renewing of your mind." The same word…

g3588.g: although, are, concern, father, for, gathered, her, household, interests, is, mother, of, profit, received, son, sons, that, the, things, those, to, what, which, Who, who, whom, whose, wife
g3588.sum: The Greek word ho is the definite article, normally translated "the." In many New Testament verses, though, it does more than point to a noun that is already there. It creates one. When the article is placed before a verb form, an adjective, a phrase, or a name, that expression becomes a person, a group, or a thing the reader can talk about. English has no single equivalent for this, so the NKJV renders these uses…

g3618.g: build, builders, building, built, edified, edifies, edify, emboldened, up
g3618.sum: Oikodoméō is the ordinary Greek verb for building: putting up a house, a barn, a tower, a tomb, or a temple. In the Gospels it usually keeps that literal sense, and Jesus uses it to tell some of His most searching parables. Two men build houses, one on rock and one on sand. A rich fool tears down his barns to build bigger ones. A man begins a tower he cannot finish. In the letters of Paul and Peter, the same verb…

g3661.w: With One Accord, With One Mind
g3661.sum: Homothymadón describes a group of people acting together with one mind, one purpose, or one shared impulse. The NKJV usually translates it "with one accord," and once "with one mind." It describes more than people standing in the same room or agreeing on paper. It pictures a company of people moved by the same inner drive and acting as one.

g3675.sum: Homóphrōn means "of one mind" or "like-minded." It describes people who share the same basic outlook, purpose, and inner direction. The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:8: "Finally, all of you be of one mind, having compassion for one another; love as brothers, be tenderhearted, be courteous." Because the word appears only there, that verse and its setting define what Peter means by it.

g3699.g: place, Where, where, whereas, Wherever, wherever, which
g3699.sum: Hópou is the Greek word behind most of the "where" and "wherever" statements in the New Testament. It points to the place, situation, or setting in which something happens. Sometimes that place is a real spot on a map, such as the Jordan crossing where John baptized. Sometimes it is an open-ended "wherever," such as the gospel going out to any place it is preached. At other times it marks a condition rather than a…

g3739.sum: Hós is the Greek word behind many of the New Testament's "who," "whom," "whose," "which," and "that." It is a relative pronoun. It points back to a person or thing just mentioned and opens a clause that tells us more about that person or thing. The NKJV says of Jesus, "This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." The word ties the Father's delight directly to the Son.

g3745.w: As Many As, Whatever, As Much As, As Long As
g3745.sum: Hósos is a Greek word of measure. It answers the questions "how many?", "how much?", "how great?", and "how long?" The NKJV renders it in many ways, most often "whatever," "as many as," "all that," "as much as," and "as long as." Whatever the English, the word draws a boundary around a group, an amount, a degree, or a stretch of time, and then says that everything inside that boundary counts. When John writes "as…

g3752.g: As, as, till, When, when, Whenever, whenever
g3752.sum: Hótan is the Greek word behind many of the New Testament's "when" and "whenever" clauses. It introduces a time frame that is real but left open. Sometimes it points to a future event that is sure to happen but has no date attached, such as the return of Christ or the coming of the Holy Spirit. At other times it describes a situation that keeps coming up, like prayer, giving, or trials, and tells us what to do each…

g3753.sum: Hóte is the Greek word usually translated "when." It introduces a clause that fixes the time of the main action, as in "when Jesus had ended these sayings," "when the Lamb opened one of the seals," or "when we were in the flesh." Most often it points to something that actually happened or a condition that actually held. That lets the biblical writers move a story into its next scene, mark the steps of a vision, and…

g3754.sum: Hóti is one of the most frequent connecting words in the Greek New Testament. It does two main jobs. First, it introduces the content of what someone says, knows, sees, or believes, much like English "that." Second, it gives a reason or explanation, usually translated "for" or "because." It can also open a direct quotation, working much like quotation marks. Because one Greek word carries both "that" and "because,"…

g3756.sum: Ou is the New Testament's ordinary word for "not" and "no." It says plainly that something is not so: an event did not happen, a claim is not true, a person is not who others suppose. The NKJV usually renders it "not" or "no," and sometimes folds it into words like "cannot," "nothing," or "never." Because it denies what is actually the case, ou does a great deal of quiet work in the Gospels and letters. It sets…

g3759.sum: Ouaí is the New Testament's cry of "Woe!" or "Alas!" It is heavy speech, never casual. On the lips of Jesus it usually announces that people stand under God's judgment: unrepentant towns, hypocritical religious leaders, the comfortable rich, and the man who would betray Him. The same word can also express pity for those caught in coming disaster, grief from those watching their world collapse, or Paul's sense of…

g3761.g: and, as, even, for, honor, Neither, neither, no, Nor, nor, Not, not, nothing, or
g3761.sum: Oudé is the New Testament's way of saying "and not." Most often it adds another item to a denial already underway, and English readers meet it as "nor" or "neither." It can also push a negative to its limit, meaning "not even." In that use it names the most surprising case that is still excluded, such as Solomon in all his glory or a whole nation privileged to know God. A third use carries a negative from one…

g3762.g: all, any, anymore, anyone, anything, despised, man, men, No, no, none, nor, not, Nothing, nothing, one, one’s
g3762.sum: Oudeís is the New Testament's word for a complete "no." It means "no one" when it points to people, "nothing" when it points to things, and "no" or "not any" when it stands beside a noun, as in "no fault." It closes off a whole group without exception. That makes it the word behind some of Scripture's most sweeping statements. "No one has seen God at any time." "Without Me you can do nothing." "I find no fault in…

g3765.g: anymore, longer, more, No, no, not, still, that
g3765.sum: Oukéti is the New Testament's way of saying "no longer." It denies something while pointing back to a time when that thing was true. Jesus had walked openly among the Jews, but after the plot against Him He "no longer" did. The Galatians had lived as slaves, but now they are "no longer" slaves but sons. g3778.sum: Hoûtos is the New Testament's ordinary word for "this" and "these." Its job is to point. It singles out a person, a thing, or an idea and holds it up so the listener cannot miss it. Sometimes it points back to someone just mentioned. Sometimes it points ahead to a statement about to be made. When it stands alone, English translations often render it simply as "he," "she," or "they."

g3842.sum: The Greek word pántote means "always," "at all times," or "on every occasion." It is a plain, everyday adverb that removes exceptions from whatever it describes. In the New Testament its weight comes from who is acting. g4012.sum: The Greek preposition perí usually points to what something is about. It ties speaking, hearing, knowing, worrying, praying, and testifying to their subject. g4074.sum: Peter was a Galilean fisherman named Simon, son of Jonah, whom Jesus called to follow Him and renamed. The name Peter (Greek Pétros ) means "a stone" or "a rock." It is the Greek form of the Aramaic Cephas , and John's Gospel spells this out: "You shall be called Cephas" (which is translated, A Stone) (John 1:42). Peter belonged to the inner circle of the Twelve. He spoke the great confession that Jesus is the…

g4166.sum: The Greek word poimḗn means a shepherd: someone who tends a flock, feeds it, leads it to pasture, and protects it from harm. In the New Testament it describes the working shepherds near Bethlehem who first heard of Christ's birth. Once, it refers to leaders Christ gives to His church, where the NKJV translates it "pastors." Its most frequent and weighty use is for Jesus Himself. He looks on the crowds with…

g4169.g: how, manner, things, What, what, Which, which
g4169.sum: Poîos is a Greek question word. It asks what or which , and often carries the sharper sense of what kind of . It appears in direct questions such as "Which is the great commandment?" and in indirect ones such as "signifying by what death He would die." g4314.sum: Prós is one of the most common prepositions in the Greek New Testament. Its basic idea is direction: something moves, speaks, or is turned toward someone or something. g4428.sum: Ptýssō is an ordinary Greek verb meaning "to fold" or "to roll up." In the New Testament it appears only once, in Luke 4:20, where Jesus rolls up the scroll of Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue. The NKJV translates it "closed": "Then He closed the book, and gave it back to the attendant and sat down."

g4571.sum: Sé is the Greek word for "you" when one person receives an action or stands at the end of a preposition. It is the singular object form: someone sees you , knows you , sends something to you . English uses the same "you" for one person or many, and for the one acting or the one acted upon, so readers often miss what the Greek makes plain. When sé appears, a single addressee is in view. In the Gospels this often…

g4572.sum: Seautoû is the Greek word for "yourself" when it is spoken to one person. It points an action, a statement, or a measure back to the person being addressed: show yourself , take heed to yourself , love your neighbor as yourself . The word appears in healing instructions, apostolic charges to Timothy and Titus, the great command to love one's neighbor, and the taunts thrown at Jesus on the cross. Readers who notice…

g4671.w: You, To You, For You, Your
g4671.sum: Soí is the Greek word for "you" when the "you" is one person and is receiving something, being spoken to, or being affected by what happens. When Jesus says to Peter, "I say to you," or the angel tells Zacharias that Elizabeth "will bear you a son," this word points the statement at one individual. It can also show belonging, as in "What is your name?", which in Greek reads roughly "What name is to you?" It also…

g4675.g: own, You, you, Your, your, Yours, yours
g4675.sum: Soû is the Greek word for "your" or "yours" when a speaker addresses one person. It is the singular "you" in the form Greek uses for belonging and relationship. Most often it attaches to a noun to show whose something is: "your prayer," "your faith," "Your name." It also appears after certain prepositions, where English needs a plain "you," as in "out of you" or "prayed for you." Occasionally it stands alone to…

g4687.g: seed, sow, sowed, sower, sown, sows
g4687.sum: Speírō is the ordinary Greek word for sowing, the farmer's work of scattering seed by hand over the ground and expecting a harvest. Jesus and the apostles took this everyday word and used it for some of the deepest realities of the kingdom of God. Jesus describes Himself and His messengers as sowers of God's word, and He describes Himself as the Son of Man sowing His people into the world. Paul uses the word for the…

g4771.g: own, sakes, You, you, Your, your, Yours, yours, yourselves
g4771.sum: This Greek pronoun is the Bible's way of turning speech toward a person and saying "you." It names the one being spoken to as the subject of a sentence, as the one who receives an action, or as the owner of something: "your name," "your prayer," "your cheek." Greek verbs already show who is acting, so when a speaker adds the pronoun as a subject, it often carries weight: you , as opposed to someone else. Peter's…

g4861.sum: Sýmpsychos describes people who are united in heart and inner life, sharing one soul together. The New Testament uses it only once, in Philippians 2:2, where Paul pleads with a church he loves: "fulfill my joy by being like-minded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind." The NKJV renders it "of one accord." Its single appearance gives it a sharp focus. Paul is describing the unity of believers who…

g4862.g: accompanied, besides, fellow, were, With, with
g4862.sum: Sýn is the Greek preposition usually translated "with." It places people or things side by side: travelers on the road, disciples gathered in prayer, a gift arriving together with a trial. Luke and Acts use it constantly to show who was present and who belonged to the company. Paul uses the same word for something deeper. Believers have died with Christ, are raised with Him, have their life hidden with Him, and will…

g4993.w: Be Of Sound Mind, Think Soberly, Be Serious
g4993.sum: The Greek verb sōphronéō means to be in one's right mind, to think clearly and soberly, and to see oneself and one's circumstances as they truly are. The New Testament uses it only six times. Those few uses cover a wide range, from a man freed from a legion of demons to an apostle measuring his own spiritual intensity for the good of a church. The NKJV renders it "in his right mind," "soberly," "of sound mind,"…

g4995.sum: Sōphronismós means a sound, steady, self-disciplined mind: the clear judgment and inner restraint that keep a person thinking rightly and acting rightly under pressure. The New Testament uses this exact word only once, in Paul's last letter, where he reminds Timothy, "For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind" (2 Timothy 1:7). Because the word appears just this once,…

g4998.sum: Sṓphrōn describes a person with a sound, well-governed mind: sensible, clear-headed and in command of desires instead of commanded by them. The NKJV translates it as "sober-minded," "temperate," and "discreet." The word does not describe a dull or timid personality. It describes an inner life in good order, one that shows itself in steady judgment and restrained conduct. Paul uses the adjective only four times, and…

g5023.g: Afterward, afterward, him, same, such, that, them, These, these, they, things, this, thus, when, words
g5023.sum: Taûta is the Greek word behind most of the New Testament's "these" and "these things." It points. Usually it points back and gathers up words, events, or teaching that have just been given, so the writer can say something about them as a whole. With the preposition meta ("after"), it forms the familiar phrase "after these things," which moves a story from one scene to the next. Because the word is neuter…

g5025.g: now, that, them, these, this, those
g5025.sum: Taútais means "these." It is a plural form of the common Greek word for "this," and it points to feminine nouns such as "days," "promises," "plagues," and "commandments." Most often it marks time, as in "in those days" or "in these days." That use ties an event to a particular stretch of the story. It also points back to something the writer has just described, so readers know exactly which promises or which plagues…

g5037.sum: The Greek word té is a joining word, usually translated "and" or "both." Its most noticeable job is to pair things: placed with kai ("and"), it forms the "both ... and" construction that holds two people, groups, or ideas together as one complete whole. When Paul says he is a debtor "both to Greeks and to barbarians," té does that binding work. Té also carries a story forward. Luke uses it often in Acts, where it…

g5100.sum: Tìs is the Greek word the New Testament uses to speak of a person or thing without naming who or what it is. g5101.sum: Tís is the Greek New Testament's question word. It asks who someone is, what something is, which of several options is meant, and, in its neuter form, why something is happening. The NKJV usually renders it "who," "whom," "whose," "what," "which," or "why." Many of the Gospels' turning points depend on this word. g5108.sum: Toioûtos points to the kind or character of something rather than simply to the thing itself. Where "this" says which one , toioûtos says what sort . g5118.g: enough, great, long, many, measure, much, things

g5118.sum: Tosoûtos measures something and points to that measure at the same time. It means "so great," "so much," "so many," or "so long," and it usually directs the reader to an amount the passage has already shown. That amount might be the size of a person's faith, the number of fish in a net, the years Jesus spent with His disciples, or the distance between Christ and the angels. g5124.sum: Toûto is the Greek word for "this" when it points to a thing, an event, or a whole idea rather than to a particular person. New Testament writers use it to look back and gather up what has just been said or done, as in "So all this was done." g5126.sum: Toûton is a Greek pointing word. It marks one particular man or one particular thing as the object of an action, and the NKJV renders it "this," "him," "this Man," or "this one." Sometimes it stands alone and points to a person: " Him they compelled to bear His cross." Other times it sits beside a noun and singles that noun out: "this bread" or "this saying." g5127.sum: Toútou is a form of the Greek word for "this." g5128.g: such, them, These, these, those, words

It can single out one member of a group ("one of the least of these commandments"). It can set a standard of comparison ("do you love Me more than these?"). It can…

g5198.sum: The Greek verb hygiaínō means to be healthy, well, or safe and sound. Luke uses it for ordinary bodily health: the sick servant found well, the prodigal son received home "safe and sound." Jesus uses it when He says, "Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick" (Luke 5:31). John uses it in his prayer that his friend Gaius would "be in health" (3 John 1:2).

g5199.sum: The Greek word hygiḗs means healthy, sound, or whole. It describes something in the condition it ought to be in, free from disease, weakness, or damage. In the New Testament it almost always describes the result when Jesus or His apostles heal someone. A withered hand is "restored as whole as the other." A man paralyzed for thirty-eight years is "made well." A beggar lame from birth "stands here before you whole."…

g5228.sum: Hypér is the Greek preposition behind many of the New Testament's most personal statements about Christ and His people. It most often means "for" in the sense of "on behalf of" or "for the sake of." Christ died for us, believers pray for one another, and Paul suffers for the churches. It can also introduce the subject someone is speaking about ("concerning"). In a different construction it means "above," "beyond,"…

g5247.sum: Hyperochē is a Greek word for standing out above others: prominence, superiority, or an elevated position. It appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul's letters, and the NKJV translates it two different ways. g5424.sum: The Greek word phrḗn means the thinking part of a person: the understanding, the capacity to reason, weigh, and judge. g5426.g: be, care, like-minded, mind, mindful, minds, observe, observes, think, understood
g5426.sum: The Greek verb phronéō means to think, but in the New Testament it usually describes the settled direction of a person's mind: what someone is intent on, what they care about, and what they live toward. It joins thought, desire, and loyalty. When Paul writes that people "set their minds" on the flesh or on the Spirit, he is describing a way of life, not a passing idea.

g5427.sum: Phrónēma is a Greek noun for a person's mindset: the settled outlook, aim, and direction of the inner life. It does not mean a passing thought or raw intelligence. It describes what a person's mind is set on and what that settled bent is reaching for. The New Testament uses it only four times, all within a few verses of Romans 8. Because the word is so rare, the setting Paul gives it carries most of its weight.

g5428.sum: Phrónēsis is a Greek word for practical understanding: the sound, morally clear judgment that knows how to live rightly. It is less about knowing many things than about seeing life truly and acting accordingly. The New Testament uses it only twice. Each use comes at a turning point in God's work of salvation.

g5590.sum: The Greek word psychē means the life of a living being and, by extension, the person who has that life. The same word can describe the life Herod wanted to take from the infant Jesus, the inner self that loves God with all its strength, the soul that God alone can destroy, and the martyrs John saw…

g737.sum: Árti is a Greek word for "now." It points to the present moment, often sharply, so that "right now" stands out against what came before or what is still to come. g846.sum: Autós is the Greek pronoun New Testament writers use most often to keep track of people and things as a passage unfolds. h1060.sum: The Hebrew word bᵉkôwr means "firstborn." In family records it usually names a father's eldest son. He held a place of honor, received a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:15–17), and was expected to lead the family after his father. In the laws of consecration it names the male that first "opens the womb" of his mother, whether human or animal (Exodus 13:2). The two uses overlap but are not identical:…

h1092.sum: Bilhan is the name of two distinct men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first was a Horite, the first-listed son of Ezer, one of the chiefs of the ancient people who lived in Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took the land (Genesis 36:27; 1 Chronicles 1:42). The second was an Israelite of the tribe of Benjamin. He was the son of Jediael and the father of seven sons, whose family line…

h110.sum: Adbeel was the third-listed of Ishmael's twelve sons and Abraham's grandson through Hagar the Egyptian. Scripture names him only twice, in Genesis 25:13 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:29, both times in the list of Ishmael's sons. The meaning of his name is uncertain. It most likely ends with ʼel , "God," and scholars have proposed meanings such as "disciplined by God" or "invited by God." None of these can be settled,…

h1106.sum: Bela is the name of four separate subjects in the Old Testament: a city on the plain near the Dead Sea, an early king of Edom, the firstborn son of Benjamin, and a later member of the tribe of Reuben. The Hebrew name בֶּלַע comes from the verb bala , "to swallow up," and is generally understood to mean "swallowing" or "destruction." Scripture never explains why any of these people or the city received the name, so…

h1160.sum: Beor is the name of two men in the Old Testament, and neither one ever speaks or acts in the biblical story. Each appears only as a father. One Beor was the father of Bela, the first king listed as reigning in Edom (Genesis 36:32; 1 Chronicles 1:43). The other was the father of Balaam, the diviner from Pethor near the Euphrates whom Balak king of Moab hired to curse Israel (Numbers 22:5). Scripture gives no reason…

h1177.sum: Baal-hanan is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first was an early king of Edom, "the son of Achbor," who reigned after a king named Saul (not Israel's Saul) and before Hadar (Genesis 36:38–39; 1 Chronicles 1:49–50). The second was Baal-hanan the Gederite, one of King David's royal stewards, who "was over the olive trees and the sycamore trees that were in the…

h121.sum: Adam was the first man, whom God formed from the dust of the ground and from whom the whole human family descends. The name is the ordinary Hebrew word for "man" or "humankind." Genesis ties it to ʼadamah , "ground," because God formed the man from the ground, and many readers also link it to the Hebrew root for "red," perhaps the color of earth or of human skin. The connection to the ground is a deliberate wordplay…

h1224.sum: Bozrah was a leading city of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, in the rugged highlands southeast of the Dead Sea. Its name comes from a Hebrew root that means to cut off, enclose, or make inaccessible, so Bozrah is generally understood to mean "enclosure," "fortress," or "fold." The name fits a stronghold that seemed out of reach. Bozrah first appears as the hometown of Jobab, one of the kings who ruled Edom…

h123.sum: Edom is first a man and then a nation. Genesis gives the name to Esau, Jacob's twin brother, and then to the people descended from him and the rugged land they held south and southeast of the Dead Sea. The name means "red." Genesis ties it directly to the moment Esau begged Jacob for "that same red stew" and sold his birthright for it (Genesis 25:30). Edom grew strong early. It had chiefs and kings "before any king…

h1323.sum: Bath is the ordinary Hebrew word for "daughter." Most often it means a man's or woman's female child or descendant. It also has wider uses. It can name the women of a people ("the daughters of Canaan"). It can describe the small towns that depend on a larger city, which the NKJV translates as "villages" or "towns." It also appears in vivid idioms. Sarah is literally "a daughter of ninety years," and the pupil of the…

h1368.g: champion, chief, commanders, excel, great, man, men, men’s, might, Mighty, mighty, one, ones, strong, valiant, valor, warrior, warriors
h1368.sum: Gibbôwr is the Hebrew word for a mighty one: a warrior, a champion, a person of exceptional strength or standing. It names Nimrod at the dawn of empire, Goliath on the field of Elah, David's elite fighters, and Boaz, the respected landowner of Bethlehem. The word itself is neither good nor bad. Everything depends on whose purposes that strength serves and where the mighty person places his trust.

h1369.g: acts, might, mighty, power, strength, victory
h1369.sum: The Hebrew word gᵉbûwrâh means might, strength, or power: the capacity to act and to carry something through. Scripture uses it for the strength of a warrior, the force of a war horse, and the military record of kings. It also uses it, far more gloriously, for the power of God. In the plural it often means God's "mighty acts," the specific occasions when His strength broke into history to save His people.

h1516.sum: The Hebrew word gayʼ means "valley." It usually names a real ravine or valley in the land of Israel: a border line in Joshua, a gate in Jerusalem's wall, or the gap between two armies. A valley is low, closed in, and hard to see into from a distance. Scripture uses those features to teach about God. Valleys became places where people hid their worst sins, where God judged, and where God showed Himself present and…

h1586.sum: Gomer is the name of two distinct figures in the Old Testament, and they must be kept apart. The first is Gomer the son of Japheth and grandson of Noah. He heads the list of Japheth's sons in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2–3; 1 Chronicles 1:5–6), and his name later stands for the people descended from him. Ezekiel names "Gomer and all its troops" among the nations that join Gog's final assault on restored Israel…

h1609.sum: Gatam was a grandson of Esau, the fourth-named son of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn by his wife Adah. He appears only in the genealogies of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 16; 1 Chronicles 1:36), where he is listed among the chiefs who headed clans in the land of Edom. The meaning of his name is uncertain, and the name tells us nothing reliable about the man himself.

h1622.sum: Girgâshîy is the Hebrew name for the Girgashites, one of the peoples descended from Canaan who lived in the land God promised to Abraham. The name appears only seven times, and never in a story of its own. No Girgashite king, city, or individual is ever named. The Girgashites appear only in lists: in the family tree of the nations, in God's promise to Abram, in the conquest under Moses and Joshua, and in a prayer of…

h1662.sum: Gath-hepher was a small town in the tribal territory of Zebulun in lower Galilee. Its name most likely means "winepress of digging" or "winepress of the well," combining the common Hebrew word gath , "winepress," with a term related to digging. Scripture names the town only twice. Joshua lists it on Zebulun's boundary, and Second Kings identifies it as the hometown of "Jonah the son of Amittai, the prophet." That…

h1666.sum: Gether is a son of Aram, grandson of Shem, and great-grandson of Noah. He appears in only two genealogical lists, the Table of Nations in Genesis 10 and the Chronicler's opening genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1. The meaning of his name is unknown. Standard Hebrew lexicons give no established derivation, and Scripture makes no wordplay on it. As a son of Aram, Gether stands at the head of one branch of the Aramean peoples…

h1710.sum: The Hebrew word dâgâh simply means "fish," usually referring to fish as a group: the living creatures of seas and rivers. It has no hidden spiritual definition. Yet Scripture uses this plain word at turning points in its story. Fish appear when God creates the world and gives humanity rule over "the fish of the sea" (Genesis 1:26, 28). They die when the Nile turns to blood (Exodus 7:18, 21). Israel remembers them…

h1719.sum: Dedan is a name the Bible uses in three ways. In the genealogies it names two different men: a son of Raamah in the line of Cush and Ham (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9), and Abraham's grandson through Keturah, a son of Jokshan (Genesis 25:3; 1 Chronicles 1:32). In the prophets it names a wealthy caravan people of northwestern Arabia. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Scholars have offered a few proposals, but…

h1721.sum: Dodanim is the name of a people descended from Javan, the son of Japheth and grandson of Noah. It appears only in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:4) and in its later restatement in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 1:7). The meaning of the name is not established. Most Hebrew scholars regard "Dodanim" as a variant spelling of "Rodanim," because the Hebrew letters d (ד) and r (ר) look almost alike and were easily confused in…

h173.sum: Aholibamah is a Hebrew personal name, usually explained as "tent of the high place." In Scripture it names two closely related things. First, it names one of Esau's wives, a woman "from the daughters of Canaan," the daughter of Anah and granddaughter of Zibeon the Hivite (Genesis 36:2). She bore Esau three sons, Jeush, Jaalam, and Korah, and each became a chief in Edom. Second, the name later appears among the…

h1732.sum: David was the youngest son of Jesse of Bethlehem. He was a shepherd boy whom God chose and Samuel anointed, and he became the second king of Israel and the first king of the line through which God promised to bring the Messiah. His name is generally understood to mean "beloved." Scripture does not build a wordplay on that meaning, and the meaning of the name should not be read as a summary of his life. His story is…

h1746.sum: Dumah is a name used for more than one subject in the Old Testament. In Genesis 25:14 and 1 Chronicles 1:30, Dumah is one of the twelve sons of Ishmael and the ancestor of an Arabian tribe. In Joshua 15:52, Dumah is a small town in the hill country of Judah. In Isaiah 21:11, "the burden against Dumah" opens a brief and mysterious oracle addressed to someone calling "out of Seir," the mountain country of Edom. The…

h1787.sum: Dishon is the name of two men in the family of Seir the Horite, the people who lived in the mountains of Seir before Esau's descendants took the land that became Edom. The first Dishon was a son of Seir and one of the Horite chiefs (Genesis 36:21, 30; 1 Chronicles 1:38). The second was a son of Anah and the brother of Aholibamah, who became one of Esau's wives (Genesis 36:25; 1 Chronicles 1:41). The name is…

h1789.sum: Dishan was a chief of the Horites, the people who lived in Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took the land. Genesis lists him as the last of the seven sons of "Seir the Horite who inhabited the land" (Genesis 36:20–21) and names his two sons, Uz and Aran (Genesis 36:28). The meaning of his name is probable rather than certain. It is closely related to dishon , a Hebrew word for a wild, clean animal of the…

h1838.sum: Dinhabah was the royal city of Bela the son of Beor, the first king of Edom named in Scripture. The meaning of the name is uncertain, and no meaning has been established. The Bible mentions Dinhabah only twice, in the list of Edom's kings (Genesis 36:32) and again in the Chronicler's genealogies (1 Chronicles 1:43). Its location is unknown.

h1847.g: knew, know, knowing, knowledge, skill, unintentionally
h1847.sum: Daʻath is the Old Testament's main word for knowledge. It can mean awareness of what one is doing, the practical know-how of a skilled craftsman, or the deep moral and spiritual understanding that comes from walking with God. Scripture never treats it as neutral information. Proverbs locates its beginning in the fear of the LORD. The first humans reached for the knowledge of good and evil on their own terms, and…

h1853.sum: Diklah is one of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:27). The Chronicler repeats his name in Israel's genealogical record (1 Chronicles 1:21). Through Joktan he descends from Shem by way of Arphaxad, Salah, and Eber. His name probably means "palm grove," a meaning drawn from a related Aramaic word for the date palm. Scripture records no deeds or words of his. Like his brothers, he…

h187.sum: Uzal was a son of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Eber, and his name appears in the two parallel lists of nations in Genesis 10:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:21. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is often associated with the idea of "going" or "departing," but the evidence does not settle the question. Like his brothers Sheba, Ophir, and Havilah, Uzal stands at the head of a people who settled toward southern…

h1877.sum: Desheʼ is the Hebrew word for fresh, young grass: the soft green growth that covers the ground after rain. The NKJV usually translates it "grass" or "herb," sometimes "tender grass," and once "green" in the familiar line "He makes me to lie down in green pastures" (Psalm 23:2). This tender growth depends on rain and light. When they come it springs up quickly, and when they are withheld it fails just as quickly.…

h1878.g: accept, anoint, ashes, fat, healthy, overflowing, prospered, rich, saturated
h1878.sum: The Hebrew verb dâshên means "to be fat" or "to make fat." In the ancient world, fatness meant richness, health, and the best portion of a thing. The same word can describe a prosperous life, a head soaked with fragrant oil, a sacrifice God receives with favor, and even the fat-soaked ashes cleared from the altar. The NKJV translates it many ways, including "accept," "anoint," "rich," "healthy," "prospered," "fat,"…

h188.sum: ʼôwy is a short Hebrew cry that names ruin and says whom it has reached. On some lips it is lament: Isaiah before the throne of God cries, "Woe is me, for I am undone!" On others it is panic, as when the Philistines learn that God has come into Israel's camp. From a prophet speaking for the Lord, it becomes a sentence of judgment: "Woe to the wicked!" Because the same cry can carry confession, terror, grief, or…

h1908.sum: Hadad is the name of at least three different Edomite men in the Old Testament. Two were early kings of Edom, listed among the rulers who reigned in the land of Esau's descendants before Israel had a king (Genesis 36:31–39; 1 Chronicles 1:43–51). The third, often called "Hadad the Edomite," is the one whose story Scripture actually tells. He was a royal child who escaped Joab's slaughter of Edom's men, grew up…

h1913.sum: Hadoram is the name of three different people in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a son of Joktan, listed among Shem's descendants in the Table of Nations, whose family settled in Arabia (Genesis 10:27; 1 Chronicles 1:21). The second is a prince of Hamath, the son of King Tou, sent with gifts of gold, silver, and bronze to congratulate David on his victory over Hadadezer (1 Chronicles…

h1945.g: Ah, Alas, Ho, O, Up, up, Woe
h1945.sum: Hôwy is the cry Israel raised over its dead, and the prophets carried that cry out of the graveyard and into the streets. Mourners said it beside a fresh tomb ("Alas, my brother!"). Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos, Habakkuk, and others spoke it over people who were still alive and prospering. When a prophet cries "Woe" over the greedy, the drunken, or the self-serving shepherd, he is announcing God's judgment in the language…

h1950.sum: Homam was a Horite, a son of Lotan and a grandson of Seir, from the people who lived in the mountains of Seir before Esau's descendants took the land. His name appears only once in the Bible, in the Chronicler's genealogy (1 Chronicles 1:39). Genesis records the same man as Hemam (Genesis 36:22), a spelling difference that reflects a common interchange of two similar Hebrew letters. The meaning of the name is…

h1980.sum: Hâlak is the ordinary Hebrew verb for going and walking. It describes Abram setting out for Canaan, rivers flowing to the sea, messengers sent on errands, and armies marching to war. From that everyday movement, Scripture draws one of its most important pictures of human life. To "walk" is to live a certain way, in a certain direction, alongside someone or after something. The few words around the verb tell you…

h20.sum: The Hebrew word ʼăbaṭṭîyach means "melon," most likely the watermelon that grew well in Egypt's sandy soil along the Nile. It names an ordinary, refreshing fruit and carries no spiritual meaning of its own. It appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 11:5. There the Israelites, tired of the manna, weep as they remember the foods of Egypt: "the fish which we ate freely in Egypt, the cucumbers, the melons, the…

h2009.g: advised, Behold, behold, course, dismay, happened, Here, here, I, Indeed, indeed, instead, Listen, Look, look, moment, Note, note, notice, Now, now, observe, right, See, see, Suddenly, suddenly, Surely, surely, surprise, surprisingly, Then, then, There, there, therefore, Watch, watch, we, well
h2009.sum: Hinnêh is the Hebrew Bible's pointing word. With it a speaker says, in effect, "Look at this," and directs the listener's attention to a person, an event, or a fact that has just come into view. The narrator uses it to put the reader inside a character's moment of discovery: Jacob waking beside Leah, or Elisha's servant seeing a mountain full of fiery chariots. God uses it when He announces what He is about to do,…

h201.sum: Omar was a grandson of Esau, listed second among the sons of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn, and he became one of the clan chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 15; 1 Chronicles 1:36). The meaning of his name is probable but not certain. It most likely comes from the Hebrew verb ʼamar , "to say" or "to speak," and is often explained as "speaker" or "eloquent." Scripture tells us nothing about his words, deeds, or faith. He…

h208.sum: Onam is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused with each other or with Onan (H0209), the son of Judah whom the LORD put to death (Genesis 38). The first Onam was a Horite, a son of Shobal, from the people who lived in Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took the land (Genesis 36:23; 1 Chronicles 1:40). The second Onam belonged to the tribe of Judah. He was a son of…

h211.sum: Ophir names both a man and a land in the Old Testament. The first is a man, a son of Joktan in the line of Shem, listed in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:29; 1 Chronicles 1:23). The second, and by far the more prominent, is a distant land so famous for its gold that "gold of Ophir" became Israel's way of naming the finest gold there was. Solomon's ships, built at Ezion Geber on the Red Sea and crewed alongside…

h2142.g: burns, commemorate, consider, dwell, earnestly, memory, mention, mindful, record, Remember, remember, remembered, remembers, remembrance, remind, still, well
h2142.sum: The Hebrew verb zâkar means "to remember." In Scripture, remembering is much more than recalling a fact. It means giving focused attention to a person, a promise or a past event in a way that leads to action. When God remembers Noah, the waters go down. When God remembers His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the Exodus begins. When Israel is told to remember the years in Egypt and the wilderness, the purpose…

h2175.sum: Zimran is a son of Abraham by Keturah. He is named first among her six sons in Genesis 25:2 and again in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1:32. Those two verses are the only places Scripture mentions him, and neither records anything he said or did. The meaning of his name is uncertain. It most likely comes from the Hebrew root zamar , which can mean "to sing" or "make music," suggesting something like "musician" or…

h2190.sum: Zaavan was a Horite, a son of Ezer and a grandson of Seir the Horite. His family lived in Mount Seir before the descendants of Esau took the land. His name probably means "trembling" or "disquieted," from a Hebrew root meaning to tremble or be agitated, though the derivation is not certain. Scripture names him only twice, in the matching genealogies of Genesis 36:27 and 1 Chronicles 1:42, and records nothing he said…

h2226.sum: Zerah is a Hebrew name shared by several different men in the Old Testament. It comes from a verb meaning "to rise," "to shine," or "to appear," the word used for the sun coming up, so the name means something like "rising" or "dawning." The best known is Zerah the son of Judah and Tamar. He was the twin whose hand came out first at birth and received the midwife's scarlet thread, only for his brother Perez to break…

h2301.sum: Hadad was the eighth listed of the twelve sons of Ishmael, which made him a grandson of Abraham through Hagar. Under this Strong's entry his name appears only once, in the Chronicler's list of Ishmael's sons (1 Chronicles 1:30). The parallel list in Genesis 25:15 names the same son "Hadar," a difference usually explained by the close resemblance of two Hebrew letters. His name comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be…

h2340.sum: "Hivite" is the name of one of the peoples living in Canaan before and during Israel's entry into the land. The word means nothing beyond the name of this people. Its importance comes from the role the Hivites play in God's dealings with Israel. Usually they appear in the familiar lists of nations God promised to drive out, and those lists repeatedly remind Israel that the land would be received by the Lord's power,…

h2341.sum: Havilah is a name the Bible uses for more than one thing. It first appears as a land in the opening chapters of Genesis, a territory encircled by the Pishon, one of the four rivers that flowed out of Eden, and Moses pauses to say that its gold "is good" and that bdellium and onyx are found there (Genesis 2:11–12). Later, the Table of Nations gives the name to two different men, a son of Cush in Ham's line (Genesis…

h2343.sum: Hul was a son of Aram and a grandson of Shem. He belongs to the generations after the Flood, listed in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10. Scripture names him only twice, in Genesis 10:23 and again in the Chronicler's genealogy at 1 Chronicles 1:17. No story is told about him. The meaning of his name is uncertain. It has been tentatively linked to the idea of a "circle" or to the Hebrew word for "sand," but neither…

h2367.sum: Husham was one of the early kings of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. Scripture says only that he came "of the land of the Temanites," that he followed Jobab of Bozrah on the throne, and that Hadad the son of Bedad succeeded him when he died (Genesis 36:34–35; 1 Chronicles 1:45–46). His name is traditionally understood to mean "haste" or "hasty," from a Hebrew root meaning to hurry, though the Bible never…

h2416.g: alive, animal, animals, beast, beasts, creature, creatures, Life, life, lifetime, Live, live, lived, lives, living, merry, nourishment, old, raw, running, thing, troop, vigorous
h2416.sum: The Hebrew word chay means "living" or "alive." It is one of the Old Testament's most common ways of speaking about life. It describes animals and wild beasts, a person's lifetime, fresh flowing water, and even raw, exposed flesh. Above all, it describes God Himself as "the living God," the One by whose life Israel swore its most solemn oaths. The same word that names the tree of life in Eden also names the fierce…

h251.g: another, associates, brethren, brother, brotherhood, brothers, brother’s, other, relative, relatives, s, these
h251.sum: The Hebrew word ʼâch means "brother." Its starting point is a male sibling, such as Cain and Abel or Joseph and his brothers. Scripture widens it to cover a nephew, a clansman, a fellow Israelite, or a fellow Levite serving at the house of God. In a common idiom, "a man to his brother," it simply means "one another." The NKJV renders it most often as "brother," "brothers," and "brethren."

h2526.sum: Ham was one of the three sons of Noah, a man who lived through the flood inside the ark and stepped out into a washed world under God's blessing. His name is usually connected with a Hebrew root meaning "warm" or "hot." That link is common but not certain, and a proposed connection with an Egyptian word for Egypt as the "black land" remains unproven. Scripture gives us only one scene from Ham's own life. After the…

h2566.sum: Hamran is a Horite, a member of the people who lived in the hill country of Seir before Esau's descendants took it over. He appears only once under this spelling, in 1 Chronicles 1:41, where he is the first-named son of Dishon. The parallel list in Genesis 36:26 calls the same man Hemdan, a separately indexed name (H2533). The meaning of Hamran is probable rather than certain. It likely comes from a Hebrew root…

h2577.sum: "Hamathite" is the name of one of the families descended from Canaan, the grandson of Noah through Ham. The word appears only twice in Scripture, both times in genealogies. Genesis 10:18 lists the Hamathite last among Canaan's sons, and 1 Chronicles 1:16 repeats the same list centuries later. The name comes from Hamath, a city on the Orontes River in what is now Syria. A Hamathite is someone who belongs to the…

h2585.sum: The Hebrew name Chănôwk belongs to four men and one city. English Bibles usually spell it "Enoch" in Genesis 4–5 and "Hanoch" elsewhere. The best known is Enoch the son of Jared, the seventh generation from Adam through Seth, the father of Methuselah, and the great-grandfather of Noah. The name is generally connected to the Hebrew verb ḥānak , "to train, dedicate, or inaugurate," so it most likely means "dedicated"…

h259.sum: ʼEchâd is the ordinary Hebrew word for "one." It counts things: one cubit, one ram, one silver platter. It also marks the first day of a month, singles out "each" curtain or "a certain" man, and pairs "one" with "the other." The NKJV renders it many ways, including "first," "each," "another," "once," "alone," and "same." Most of its uses are plain counting, and many cluster in the detailed instructions for Israel's…

h2637.g: decreased, deprive, dry, fail, lack, lacked, lacks, less, lower, needs, want
h2637.sum: Châçêr is the Hebrew verb for lacking, falling short, or running low. It can describe floodwaters going down, a number coming up short, a jar of oil running dry, or a person going without bread. It names the gap between what is needed and what is on hand. Scripture uses this ordinary word to make some of its most comforting promises: "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want" (Psalm 23:1).

h2660.sum: Hepher is a Hebrew name that most likely means "pit" or "well." It comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to search out." The Old Testament uses it for several unrelated people and places, and they should not be merged. The most important is Hepher the Manassite, a son of Gilead and the father of Zelophehad. When Zelophehad died in the wilderness with five daughters and no sons, his family line seemed headed for…

h269.sum: The Hebrew word ʼâchôwth means "sister." Most often it names an actual female sibling, such as Miriam watching over baby Moses, Rachel envying Leah, Dinah avenged by her brothers, or Tamar wronged by her half-brother Amnon. Hebrew also uses the word in an everyday phrase, literally "a woman to her sister," to say that things are joined "one to another." Scripture uses this phrase for the coupled curtains of the…

h2700.sum: Hazarmaveth is a son of Joktan and a great-great-great-grandson of Shem. He appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the list of Noah's descendants known as the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). His name joins two Hebrew words, chatsar , "court," "village," or "settlement," and maveth , "death," so it means "Court of Death" or "Village of Death." Scripture never explains why anyone would…

h275.sum: Ahuzzam was a man of the tribe of Judah, named only once in Scripture, at 1 Chronicles 4:6. He was a son of Ashhur, "the father of Tekoa," and Ashhur's wife Naarah, and his name heads the list of her four sons. His name comes from the Hebrew verb meaning "to grasp" or "to take possession," and it probably means "possessor" or "their possession." The exact sense is uncertain. Scripture tells us nothing about his…

h2753.sum: Hori is a Hebrew proper name connected with the ancient Horites, the people who lived in the rugged hill country of Mount Seir, south of the Dead Sea, before Esau's descendants took the land. Under this one Strong's entry stand three distinct realities: Hori the son of Lotan, a grandson of "Seir the Horite" (Genesis 36:22; 1 Chronicles 1:39); the Horite people and their chiefs as a group (Genesis 36:20, 30;…

h28.sum: Abida was a grandson of Abraham through Midian, one of the six sons Abraham had with Keturah. He appears only twice in Scripture, both times in a list: "the sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abidah, and Eldaah" (Genesis 25:4; 1 Chronicles 1:33). The NKJV spells his name "Abidah" in Genesis and "Abida" in Chronicles, but the Hebrew name is the same. It is built from the words for "father" and "to know," and…

h2845.sum: Heth is named in the Bible's family table of nations as a son of Canaan, listed right after Canaan's firstborn, Sidon (Genesis 10:15; 1 Chronicles 1:13). His name lives on mainly through his descendants, "the sons of Heth" and "the daughters of Heth," a Canaanite community living around Hebron in the days of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The name is often connected with a Hebrew root meaning "to be shattered" or "to be…

h2896.sum: Ṭôwb is the Old Testament's ordinary word for "good." It covers a wide range: a ripe fig, a handsome young man, a merry heart, a fertile land, wise advice, a righteous life, and the character of God Himself. At its heart the word describes something that is as it ought to be, whether useful, pleasing, beneficial, or right. Context decides which of these is meant. The same word that calls Rebekah "very beautiful to…

h2983.sum: The Hebrew word translated "Jebusite" names a Canaanite people who lived in the central hill country and held the city of Jebus, later known as Jerusalem. It is a people name and carries no hidden meaning. The Jebusites first appear in the table of nations, then in God's repeated lists of peoples whose land He promised to Abraham and his descendants. Long after Israel entered Canaan, they still held Jerusalem. Judah…

h3050.sum: Yâhh (Yah) is a short, poetic form of God's personal name, Yahweh, the name God revealed to Israel as the One who rescues and stays with His people. In most English Bibles it is hidden behind the capitalized word "LORD." The NKJV prints "YAH" in a few places, such as Psalm 68:4, Isaiah 12:2, Isaiah 26:4, and Isaiah 38:11. The shortened name appears mainly in songs and prayers. It first appears in Israel's song at…

h3103.sum: Jobab is a Hebrew name shared by at least five different men in the Old Testament. One is a son of Joktan in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:29). Another is an early king of Edom from the city of Bozrah (Genesis 36:33–34). A third is the king of Madon who joined Jabin of Hazor against Joshua (Joshua 11:1). The last two are Benjamites named in the Chronicler's family records (1 Chronicles 8:9, 18). The meaning of…

h3117.sum: The Hebrew word yôwm means "day." It can name a full day, evening and morning together, the hours of daylight, or "today." It can also stretch to cover a lifetime ("all the days of my life"), an era ("in the days of the judges"), or a habit ("day by day"). Context decides which one is meant, and the Old Testament uses the word in every one of its books.

h3120.sum: Javan is first a man and then a people. Genesis names him as the fourth-listed son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah. His descendants spread through the "coastlands," the islands and shores of the Mediterranean, and in later Scripture his name stands for the Greek world. The name is the Hebrew equivalent of the Greek word for the Ionians, the Greeks of the Aegean coast and islands who were the first Greeks most Near…

h3195.sum: Jetur was a son of Ishmael and a grandson of Abraham through Hagar. He is listed tenth among Ishmael's twelve sons (Genesis 25:15; 1 Chronicles 1:31), and his name later identifies a people descended from him who lived east of the Jordan. The name probably means "enclosure" or "encampment," perhaps the circular camp of a herding people, though the derivation is not certain. Scripture records no words or deeds of…

h3205.sum: Yâlad is the ordinary Hebrew verb for bringing new life into the world. A mother bears a child, a father begets a son, a child is born, and a midwife helps bring the baby out. Because every family line runs through birth, this is the word that drives the genealogies of Genesis and Chronicles. Its long chains of "begot" record how God kept His promise alive from Adam to David, generation after generation of people…

h3266.sum: Jeush is the name of four different men in the Bible, and they should not be confused with one another. The first is an Edomite chief, a son of Esau by his wife Aholibamah (Genesis 36:18; 1 Chronicles 1:35). The second is a Gershonite Levite, a son of Shimei, listed in David's organization of the Levites (1 Chronicles 23:10–11). The third is a Benjaminite from King Saul's family line through Jonathan (1 Chronicles…

h3281.sum: Jaalam was a son of Esau by his wife Aholibamah. He was born in the land of Canaan and later became a clan chief among Esau's descendants in Edom (Genesis 36:5, 14, 18; 1 Chronicles 1:35). His name probably means "concealed" or "hidden." It comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to hide," though the derivation is not absolutely certain. Scripture says nothing of his deeds, words, or faith. What it preserves is his place…

h3292.sum: Jaakan was a son of the Horite chief Ezer and a descendant of Seir the Horite. These were the people who lived in the hill country of Seir before Esau's descendants took it over. Scripture names him only once under this spelling, in the Chronicler's list of Seir's family: "The sons of Ezer were Bilhan, Zaavan, and Jaakan" (1 Chronicles 1:42). The parallel list in Genesis 36:27 names the same man as Akan, a…

h3315.sum: Japheth was one of the three sons of Noah, a brother of Shem and Ham, who entered the ark with his wife and survived the flood. His name is connected to the Hebrew idea of being open, wide, or spacious, so it is commonly understood as "enlarged" or "he will enlarge." Genesis itself makes the link through wordplay when Noah prays, "May God enlarge Japheth" (Genesis 9:27). His name appears only eleven times, all in…
