h3318.sum: Yâtsâʼ is one of the Old Testament's everyday verbs of movement. It means to go out or come out of a place, and in its causative use it means to bring someone or something out. People go out of tents, cities, and countries. Armies go out to battle. Slaves go out free. Children come from their parents' bodies, plants come up from the ground, water flows from a source, and words come out of a mouth. The word points to…

h3327.sum: Isaac was the son God promised to Abraham and Sarah long after they were too old to have children. He married Rebekah, became the father of Esau and Jacob, and is the middle name in the title God gave Himself: "the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." His name means "he laughs" or "laughter," from the Hebrew verb for laughing. Genesis builds his story around that word. Abraham fell on his face and laughed at the…

h3336.g: formed, frame, imagination, inclination, intent, mind, mold
h3336.sum: The Hebrew word yêtser means "something formed." Sometimes it refers to a physical thing that has been shaped, such as a clay pot, a carved idol, or the human body made from dust. More often it refers to what the heart forms inwardly: the settled bent of a person's thoughts, purposes and desires. The NKJV translates it as "intent," "imagination," "inclination," "mind," "frame," "formed," and "mold." It appears only…

h3355.sum: Joktan was a son of Eber and a descendant of Shem who lived in the generations after the flood. Genesis introduces him beside his brother Peleg, "for in his days the earth was divided" (Genesis 10:25). His name is generally connected with a Hebrew root meaning "small," "little," or "younger." That derivation is probable rather than certain, and Scripture itself never explains the name. Joktan appears only in the…

h3370.sum: Jokshan was a son of Abraham by Keturah, the woman Abraham took after the account of Sarah's death and Isaac's marriage. He was the second listed of Keturah's six sons, and Scripture remembers him chiefly as the father of Sheba and Dedan, names later tied to the trading peoples of Arabia (Genesis 25:2–3; 1 Chronicles 1:32). The meaning of his name is uncertain. It is often connected with a Hebrew verb meaning "to…

h3372.g: acts, afraid, awesome, dared, deeds, dreadful, Fear, fear, feared, Fearful, fearfully, fearing, fears, frighten, revere, reverence, saw, see, terrible, things
h3372.sum: Yârêʼ is the ordinary Hebrew verb for fear, and it covers the whole range of that experience. It describes a soldier shaking before an enemy, a guilty man hiding from God, a worshiper bowing in reverent awe, and a child honoring his parents. Some forms describe what causes fear, so the same word can call God, His deeds, or His coming day "awesome," "terrible," or "dreadful." The word never shrinks to mere…

h3382.sum: Jared is a name the Hebrew Bible gives to two different men. The better known is the patriarch before the Flood: the son of Mahalalel, the father of Enoch, and the sixth generation from Adam through Seth (Genesis 5:15–20; 1 Chronicles 1:2). The second is a much later man of Judah, called "the father of Gedor" in a difficult genealogy of that tribe (1 Chronicles 4:18). The name comes from the Hebrew verb yarad , "to…

h3392.sum: Jerah was a son of Joktan in the line of Shem. His name appears only twice in Scripture, both times in a list of Joktan's thirteen sons (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). The name means "moon" or "month." In form it is the same as the Hebrew word for "month," and it is closely related to the word for "moon." Jerah is best understood as both a man and the ancestor of a people. Genesis places Joktan's descendants in…

h3435.sum: Ishbak was one of the six sons Abraham fathered through Keturah, whose family Genesis records after the account of Sarah's burial and Isaac's marriage. He is named only twice in Scripture, both times in a list of his brothers (Genesis 25:2; 1 Chronicles 1:32). Nothing he said or did is recorded. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Some connect it to a root meaning "to leave" or "to forsake," but that link is…

h345.sum: Aiah is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and neither one ever speaks or acts on the page. The first is a Horite, a son of Zibeon, listed among the original peoples of Mount Seir in the genealogies of Genesis 36:24 and 1 Chronicles 1:40. The second is an Israelite known only as the father of Rizpah, the concubine of King Saul (2 Samuel 3:7; 21:8, 10, 11). The name is Hebrew and means "bird of…

h3458.sum: Ishmael is a Hebrew name meaning "God hears" or "God will hear." Six different men carry it in the Old Testament, and two of them stand out. The first and most important is Ishmael, son of Abraham and Hagar, the Egyptian servant of Sarah. He was born when Abram and Sarai tried to obtain God's promised heir by their own arrangement. God gave him his name before he was born, because "the LORD has heard your…

h3478.sum: Israel is the name God gave to Jacob, son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham. Through his twelve sons it became the name of an entire people. Across the Old Testament, "Israel" can mean the patriarch himself, the twelve-tribe nation descended from him, the land God gave them, and, after Solomon's kingdom split, the ten northern tribes as distinct from Judah. The prophets can also address Judah and Jerusalem as Israel,…

h3506.sum: Ithran is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a Horite, a son of Dishon (Genesis 36:26; 1 Chronicles 1:41) among "the sons of Seir the Horite who inhabited the land" (Genesis 36:20). The Horites lived in the mountains of Seir before the descendants of Esau took the region, which came to be called Edom (Deuteronomy 2:12). The second is an Israelite of the…

h3509.sum: Jetheth was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He appears only twice in Scripture, in the list of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:40 and in its repetition in 1 Chronicles 1:51. Genesis presents these chiefs "according to their families and their places," so the name Jetheth seems to stand for both a clan leader and the clan or district that carried his name somewhere in the region of Mount Seir.…

h3563.sum: Kôwç is the ordinary Hebrew word for a cup, the vessel a king, a servant, or a poor man in his hut would lift to his lips. Scripture lets this everyday object carry a great deal. Someone who hands you a cup has decided what you will drink, so the cup became a natural picture of a person's lot in life, the portion measured out and placed in a person's hands. David can say of the Lord, "You are the portion of my…

h3568.sum: The Bible uses Cush for different people and lands, whose histories should be distinguished. Most often it names the land and people south of Egypt along the upper Nile, roughly ancient Nubia and today's northern Sudan, which the NKJV usually renders "Ethiopia." The same name belongs to a son of Ham and grandson of Noah, the ancestor listed first among Ham's sons and the father of Nimrod (Genesis 10:6–8). It also…

h3667.g: Canaan, Canaanite, merchant, trade, trader, traders
h3667.sum: Canaan is first a man and then a land. Genesis introduces him as the son of Ham and grandson of Noah, the one on whom Noah pronounced a curse after Ham's shameful act in the tent (Genesis 9:18–27). His descendants, including Sidon, Heth, and the peoples later known as Jebusites, Amorites, Hivites and others, settled the territory between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean Sea. That territory took his name. The…

h3695.sum: Casluhim is the name of an ancient people listed among the descendants of Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt, in the family tree of nations that grew from Noah's sons after the flood. The name appears only twice in the Bible, in Genesis 10:14 and in the repeated genealogy of 1 Chronicles 1:12. The Casluhim never appear in a story, a prophecy, or a psalm. What makes them matter is the short note attached to their…

h3732.sum: Kaphtôrîy is the Hebrew name for the people of Caphtor, called the "Caphtorim" in the NKJV. It appears only three times in the Old Testament. Two of these are in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:14, repeated in 1 Chronicles 1:12), which lists the Caphtorim among the descendants of Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt, and places them close to the Philistines. The third is a short historical note in Deuteronomy 2:23, which…

h3763.sum: Cheran was a Horite, one of the original inhabitants of Mount Seir, the rugged highland south of the Dead Sea that later became the land of Edom. He appears only in two parallel genealogies, Genesis 36:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:41. Both name him last among the four sons of Dishon within the Horite clan genealogy; this Dishon is most naturally read as the chief who was a son of Seir. The meaning of his name is uncertain.…

h3794.sum: Kittîy is the Hebrew name for Kittim, a people descended from Javan, and for the island of Cyprus where they settled. Over time the name came to stand for the distant western coastlands of the Mediterranean, the sea peoples and naval powers beyond the horizon of Israel's world. The NKJV renders the same Hebrew word two ways. It keeps "Kittim" in the genealogies of Genesis and 1 Chronicles and uses "Cyprus" in the…

h3820.sum: Lêb is the Old Testament's main word for the heart, and it covers far more than the English word usually does. A modern reader thinks of the heart as feelings, set against the "head." A Hebrew reader made no such split. The heart was where a person thought, understood, decided, desired, grieved, and rejoiced. That is why the NKJV sometimes renders lêb as "mind," "understanding," or "will," and why Proverbs describes…

h3824.g: anger, breasts, come, Consider, consider, courage, diligent, encouragement, fainthearted, heart, hearts, inexperienced, mind, understanding, unknown, wholehearted
h3824.sum: The Hebrew word lêbâb means "heart," but the Bible's heart is far more than the place where feelings live. It is the inner control center of a person: where we think, remember, decide, fear, take courage, worship, and give our loyalty. When Moses tells Israel to love the LORD "with all your heart," he is claiming the whole inner life for God, including attention, intentions, and allegiance. Scripture uses this word…

h3853.sum: Lehabim is the name of an ancient people descended from Mizraim, the biblical name for Egypt, who was a son of Ham. The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the same line of the "Table of Nations": "Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim" (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). It carries no theological meaning of its own. It names a family of peoples who settled in and around the Nile Valley…

h3865.sum: Lud is first a person and then a people. Genesis names him as a son of Shem, listed with his brothers Elam, Asshur, Arphaxad, and Aram (Genesis 10:22; 1 Chronicles 1:17). The prophets later use the same name for a distant nation known for its soldiers, and English translations often render it "Lydia." Since ancient times that nation has been identified with the Lydians of western Asia Minor, though Scripture itself…

h3866.sum: Lûwdîy is the Hebrew name for the Ludim, an ancient people whom Scripture places in the family of Egypt. The word appears only three times. Two are in the great list of nations, where "Mizraim begot Ludim" (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). The third is in Jeremiah's prophecy against Egypt, where the NKJV renders the word "Lydians" and describes them as the warriors "who handle and bend the bow" (Jeremiah 46:9).…

h3877.sum: Lotan was a chief of the Horites, the people who lived in the mountain country of Seir before the descendants of Esau took it over. He is named first among the sons of Seir the Horite (Genesis 36:20; 1 Chronicles 1:38), and his own sons were Hori and Hemam, called Homam in Chronicles. The meaning of his name is not certain. It probably comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to wrap" or "to cover," the same root behind…

h3884.g: If, if, not, that, Unless, unless
h3884.sum: This Hebrew word opens a door onto something that never happened. It introduces a condition contrary to fact, usually in the past: "If this had not been so…" The sentence that follows describes the result that would have come, and that result is almost always disaster. The NKJV renders it "unless," "if… not," or "were it not that." Most often the speaker is looking back with relief or gratitude: Israel would have…

h39.sum: Abimael is one of the thirteen sons of Joktan, a descendant of Shem through Arphaxad, Salah, and Eber. He appears only twice in Scripture, both times as a single name in a list: once in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:28) and once in the Chronicler's matching genealogy (1 Chronicles 1:22). His name most likely means "My Father is God (El)," though the exact force of the middle syllable is debated. Some scholars…

h3929.sum: Lamech is the name of two different men who lived before the Flood. They stand at turning points in two very different family lines. The first Lamech belongs to the family of Cain, and he is the seventh generation from Adam through that line (Genesis 4:18–24). He took two wives, fathered the founders of herding, music, and metalworking, and then composed a song boasting that he had killed a young man for wounding…

h3966.sum: The Hebrew word mᵉʼôd is the Old Testament's ordinary word for "very," "greatly," and "exceedingly." It turns up the volume on whatever it touches: a city's wickedness, a famine's severity, a father's grief, a king's terror, or the greatness of God. On its own it carries no moral weight. It intensifies, and the Bible's writers choose carefully what they intensify. The same word that marks God's verdict on finished…

h4014.sum: Mibzar was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He is named only twice, in the closing list of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:42 and again in the Chronicler's copy of that list in 1 Chronicles 1:53. The name means "fortress" or "fortified place." It is the same word Hebrew uses for a stronghold or walled city. Genesis says these chiefs were listed "according to their families and their places"…

h4017.sum: Mibsam is the name of two different men in the Old Testament genealogies. The first, and better known, is the fourth-listed son of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. He is listed among the twelve sons who became tribal chiefs in the Arabian wilderness (Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29). h4025.sum: Magdiel was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. His name appears only twice in Scripture: in the closing roster of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:43 and in the Chronicler's retelling of that list in 1 Chronicles 1:54. The name is a compound of a Hebrew word for "excellence" or "choice thing" and El , "God," so it most likely means "choice gift of God" or "preciousness of…

h4031.sum: Magog appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, yet few names travel farther. It begins as the name of the second-listed son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, listed among the peoples who spread across the earth after the Flood (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). Centuries later, Ezekiel uses it for a distant northern land whose ruler, Gog, leads a vast army against God's restored people (Ezekiel 38–39). Finally,…

h4074.sum: Mâday names two closely linked things in the Hebrew Bible. First, it is Madai, a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah, listed among the founding peoples in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). Second, and far more often, it is Media and the Medes, the people and land in the mountains of what is now northwestern Iran. Over time the Medes became a major world power and later partners with Persia. The…

h4080.sum: Midian is the name of a son of Abraham, of the people descended from him, and of the desert land where they lived, chiefly east of the Gulf of Aqaba and ranging across the wilderness south and east of Canaan. The name most likely comes from a Hebrew root meaning "strife," "contention," or "judgment." That derivation is probable rather than certain, and Scripture never builds a lesson on it. h4091.sum: Medan was one of the six sons born to Abraham through Keturah, whose marriage Genesis records after the account of Sarah's death. He is named only in two family lists, Genesis 25:2 and 1 Chronicles 1:32. His name is usually connected with a Hebrew word meaning "strife" or "contention," related to a root that means to judge or contend. That meaning is a probable derivation, not a certain one, and Scripture never…

h4105.sum: Mehetabel is a Hebrew name meaning "God does good" or "God benefits." Two different people in Scripture bear it, living many centuries apart. The first is a queen of Edom, the wife of King Hadar (spelled Hadad in Chronicles). Genesis 36:39 and 1 Chronicles 1:50 both name her among the early kings of Esau's descendants. h4111.sum: Mahalalel is the name of two men in the Old Testament. The better known is the patriarch of Genesis 5. He was the son of Cainan, the father of Jared, and the fifth generation from Adam through Seth. The name means "Praise of God" or "God's praise." It joins the Hebrew word for praise with El , God. Scripture records only his birth, his fatherhood, his 895 years, and his death. Yet his place in the line running from…

h4124.sum: Moab is the name of a man, the nation descended from him, and the land that nation occupied east of the Dead Sea. The first Moab was the son of Lot by his elder daughter, born in the cave after the destruction of Sodom (Genesis 19:37). His descendants became a settled kingdom across the Jordan from Israel. h4191.sum: Mûwth is the ordinary Hebrew verb for dying. It describes a person or animal coming to the end of life, and in other forms it means to kill, execute, or put to death. Scripture uses it in genealogies, battle reports, courtroom laws, priestly warnings, and the laments of Job and Ecclesiastes. Wherever life ends in the Old Testament, this word is usually present.

h4195.sum: Môwthâr is a Hebrew word for what is left over: the surplus, gain, or advantage that remains when the account is settled. It appears only three times in the Old Testament, all in the wisdom books. In Proverbs it names the real "profit" and "plenty" that come from honest labor and careful planning, set against the "poverty" that follows empty talk and hasty shortcuts. In Ecclesiastes the same word takes on a heavier…

h4199.sum: Mizzah was a grandson of Esau, the fourth-listed son of Reuel and Basemath's grandson, and he became one of the chiefs of Edom. His name appears only three times, all in family records (Genesis 36:13, 17; 1 Chronicles 1:37). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Strong's tentatively connects it to an unused root meaning to faint with fear, but the evidence is too thin to build anything on, and it may simply have…

h420.sum: Eldaah was a grandson of Abraham through Keturah. He was the last of the five sons of Midian listed in Genesis 25:4 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:33. His name joins El , "God," with a second element whose root is debated. It probably means "God has known," though some scholars read it as "God has called" or "God of knowledge." No other person in Scripture bears this name, and he does nothing in the biblical record…

h4210.sum: The Hebrew word mizmôwr means a psalm, a song set to music. The NKJV translates it "Psalm," and every one of its occurrences is in the Book of Psalms, always in the heading above a psalm, never inside the poem itself. When a heading reads "A Psalm of David," this is the word at work. It tells the reader what kind of text follows: a composition meant to be sung, most likely with instruments.

h425.sum: Elah is a Hebrew name meaning "terebinth," a large, long-lived tree common in the land of Israel and sometimes rendered "oak" in English Bibles. The name belongs to one famous place and several different people, and keeping them separate is essential. The best known is the Valley of Elah, a broad valley in the foothills of Judah where Saul's army faced the Philistines and young David killed Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2,…

h4284.g: artistic, devices, devised, invented, means, plan, Plans, plans, plot, purpose, purposes, scheme, schemes, thoughts, works
h4284.sum: Machăshâbâh is the Hebrew word for what the mind produces: a thought, an intention, a plan, a scheme, or a skilled design. It describes the inner work of thinking something through before it becomes action. Scripture uses it for the corrupt thoughts of the human heart before the flood, for Haman's plot to destroy the Jews, and for the artistic designs God's Spirit gave Bezalel for the tabernacle. Most strikingly, it…

h4308.sum: Matred was a member of an Edomite family remembered in Scripture only through a royal marriage. When Hadar (spelled Hadad in Chronicles) became king of Edom, the record names his wife Mehetabel as "the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab" (Genesis 36:39; compare 1 Chronicles 1:50). Matred is most often understood to be Mehetabel's mother, though the wording has been read in more than one way. The name is…

h4314.sum: Mezahab is named only in the royal record of Edom, as the ancestor of Mehetabel, wife of Hadar (called Hadad in Chronicles), the eighth king listed in Edom (Genesis 36:39; 1 Chronicles 1:50). His name means "waters of gold," a Hebrew compound of the words for "waters" and "gold." Scripture never explains why he bore the name, and it records nothing he did. He appears in Edom's king-list, which Genesis introduces as…

h4325.g: Brook, flood, floodwater, floodwaters, for, places, pool, rains, sea, washing, waste, Water, water, watercourses, watering, waterless, waters, watersprings, wellsprings
h4325.sum: Mayim is the ordinary Hebrew word for water. It names the water a traveler drinks, the water a priest washes with, the rain that falls on the fields, the river Israel crossed, and the deep that covered the earth before God spoke light into being. The word itself means nothing more than "water." Scripture, however, returns to it so often and in so many settings that water becomes one of the Bible's richest pictures…

h4428.g: King, king, kingdom, Kings, kings, King’s, king’s, looking, Milcom, of, reign, royal, s
h4428.sum: Melek is the ordinary Hebrew word for "king." It names the man who sits at the top of a people's authority. That might be the ruler of a small Canaanite town, the emperor of Assyria or Persia, or a son of David on the throne in Jerusalem. The same word is also used of the LORD Himself. When the psalmist sings, "The LORD is King forever and ever" (Psalm 10:16), he uses the same word the historians use for Pharaoh and…

h4496.g: comforting, easily, place, places, quartermaster, rest, resting, still
h4496.sum: Mᵉnûwchâh is the Hebrew word for rest: a settled, secure condition, or the place where that settled life is found. It describes more than a break from work. A young widow finds it in a husband's home, Israel finds it in the land God promised, and the soul finds it beside the "still waters" of Psalm 23. Most strikingly, God Himself speaks of a resting place. David wanted to build Him a "house of rest," and in Psalm…

h4506.sum: Manahath is a name the Bible uses in two ways. It belongs to a Horite man, a son of Shobal, who lived among the original inhabitants of Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took that land (Genesis 36:23; 1 Chronicles 1:40). It is also the name of a town or clan district in Israel. In Judah's genealogy, the "Manahethites" are counted among the families descended from Shobal and Salma, grandsons of Caleb son of Hezron…

h4570.sum: Maʻgâl is a Hebrew word for a track or worn path, the kind of established course left in the ground by repeated travel. In the historical books it names the circular camp of Saul's army. In the Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah it becomes a picture of a person's course of life. Most English readers know it from one of the best-loved lines in Scripture: "He leads me in the paths of righteousness For His name's sake"…

h464.sum: Eliphaz is the name of two different men in the Old Testament, and both belong to the world of Edom. The first is Esau's firstborn son by his wife Adah. His sons became chiefs of Edom, and through his concubine Timna he became the father of Amalek, whose descendants were Israel's bitter enemy for centuries (Genesis 36:10–12; 1 Chronicles 1:35–36). The second is Eliphaz the Temanite, the first and leading speaker…

h4714.sum: Egypt, in Hebrew Mitsrayim , is the ancient land and nation of the Nile valley southwest of Canaan. It is one of the most frequently named places in the Old Testament. The same Hebrew name first appears as Mizraim, a son of Ham, whose descendants are listed among the nations in Genesis 10. The name is commonly explained as meaning "double straits" or "two distresses." Its dual-looking ending is often linked to the…

h473.sum: Elishah appears only three times in the Bible, but those three verses reach from the scattering of the nations after the Flood to the prophetic lament over Tyre. In Genesis 10:4 and 1 Chronicles 1:7, Elishah is the first-named son of Javan, a grandson of Japheth and great-grandson of Noah. His line is among those from whom "the coastland peoples of the Gentiles were separated into their lands" (Genesis 10:5). By…

h4832.g: conciliation, healing, health, incurable, remedy, sound, wholesome
h4832.sum: The Hebrew noun marpêʼ means healing, health, cure, or remedy. It describes the condition of something that has been made whole again, and Scripture applies it to a sick body, a troubled heart, a strained relationship, and a nation broken under God's judgment. English versions translate it in several ways: "health," "healing," "remedy," "wholesome," "sound," and once, in a conflict with a ruler, "conciliation."

h4854.sum: Massa was the seventh-listed of the twelve sons of Ishmael, which makes him a grandson of Abraham through Hagar the Egyptian. Scripture names him only twice, both times in the family record of Ishmael (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). Like his brothers, he gave his name to a people, one of the "twelve princes according to their nations" who settled in the deserts of northern Arabia (Genesis 25:16). His name is…

h486.sum: Almodad is the first-named son of Joktan in the Table of Nations. Joktan was a son of Eber and a descendant of Shem through Arphaxad and Salah. Almodad appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the same list: "Joktan begot Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah" (Genesis 10:26; 1 Chronicles 1:20). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Some interpret it in Hebrew as something like "God is a friend" or "measure of…

h4902.sum: Meshech first appears in Scripture as a son of Japheth and grandson of Noah (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). It then becomes the name of the people descended from him, a distant northern nation usually paired with Tubal. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It sounds like a Hebrew verb meaning "to draw" or "to drag," and some have connected it with drawing a bow. It is more likely the Hebrew form of a foreign…

h4927.sum: Mishma is the name of two different men in the Bible's family records. The first is the fifth-listed son of Ishmael, a brother of Mibsam, listed among the twelve princes who descended from Abraham through Hagar (Genesis 25:14; 1 Chronicles 1:30). The second is a man from the tribe of Simeon, the son (not the brother) of Mibsam and father of Hamuel (1 Chronicles 4:25–26). The name comes from the Hebrew verb shama ,…

h4938.sum: The Hebrew word mishʻênâh means a support, something a person leans on. Most often it is a walking-stick or staff: the stick an injured man uses to walk outside again, the staff an old woman holds as she sits in a Jerusalem street, the staff of a shepherd. Once it means something you cannot hold in your hand. In Isaiah 3:1 it describes the bread and water a city leans on to stay alive.

h4957.sum: Masrekah was a town in ancient Edom, the land settled by Esau's descendants in the mountains of Seir south and east of the Dead Sea. Scripture names it twice, in one narrative notice preserved in two parallel records: "When Hadad died, Samlah of Masrekah reigned in his place" (Genesis 36:36; 1 Chronicles 1:47). The name probably means "vineyard" or "place of choice vines." It appears to come from the same Hebrew…

h4968.sum: Methuselah was the son of Enoch, the father of Lamech, and the grandfather of Noah. He belongs to the line of Seth that Genesis 5 traces from Adam to the Flood. He is best known as the longest-lived person in Scripture: "So all the days of Methuselah were nine hundred and sixty-nine years; and he died" (Genesis 5:27). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Many scholars read it as "man of the dart" or "man of the…

h5032.sum: Nebaioth was the firstborn son of Ishmael and a grandson of Abraham through Hagar. His name also became the name of the Arabian tribe that descended from him, a pastoral people of the eastern deserts known for their flocks. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It has often been linked to ideas such as "heights," "prominences," or "fruitfulness," but none of these is settled, and Scripture itself offers no…

h5095.g: fed, guide, guided, lead, leads, ride
h5095.sum: The Hebrew verb nâhal means to lead or guide, and it usually describes a leader who takes responsibility for the well-being of those who follow. It appears only ten times in the Old Testament. NKJV renders it "lead," "guide," "guided," and "leads," and in two places it reads "fed" and "ride." Jacob uses it of moving his weary flocks and young children at a pace they could bear. The narrative uses it of Joseph…

h5104.g: Brook, flood, floods, River, river, rivers, riverside, streams, waters
h5104.sum: Nâhâr is the ordinary Hebrew word for a river, usually a substantial flowing watercourse. Scripture uses it for the river that watered Eden, for the Nile and its channels, for the rivers of Damascus and Babylon, and especially for the Euphrates, which is so often called simply "the River." In poetry the plural can describe surging waters, so the NKJV sometimes translates it "floods." The same word therefore names…

h5116.g: dwelling, fold, folds, habitation, haunts, home, lovely, pastures, place, remains, sheepfold, stable
h5116.sum: The Hebrew word nâveh means a settled place to live. It is often a shepherd's word for the pasture or fold where a flock is brought to rest, and it also describes the homes of people, the dens of wild animals, and the holy dwelling of God. It is the word behind the "green pastures" of Psalm 23, the "good fold" of Ezekiel 34, and the "holy habitation" toward which God led Israel after the Red Sea (Exodus 15:13). It…

h5146.sum: Noah, son of Lamech, stands at the hinge between the world before the Flood and the world after it. He was the tenth generation from Adam through Seth, the father of Shem, Ham, and Japheth, and the man through whom God preserved human life when He judged a world "filled with violence" (Genesis 6:11). His name, Nôach, is generally understood to mean "rest." Genesis explains it with a related-sounding word: at his…

h5148.g: brings, brought, deployed, forth, govern, guide, guided, guides, Lead, lead, leads, led, put, stationed
h5148.sum: Nâchâh is the Hebrew verb for leading or guiding someone along a way to a destination. Most often God is the one who leads. He led Israel out of Egypt by the pillar of cloud and fire. He led His flock as a shepherd. And He answers the believer who prays, "Lead me." The word can also describe ordinary human guiding, such as a man escorting his parents to safety, a gift opening a door before great men, or troops…

h5152.sum: Nahor is the name of two men in Abraham's family, and the reader has to keep them apart. The first Nahor was Abraham's grandfather, the son of Serug and the father of Terah, listed in the line from Shem to Abram (Genesis 11:22–25; 1 Chronicles 1:26). Luke's genealogy of Jesus later passes through this man (Luke 3:34). The second Nahor was Abraham's brother, a son of Terah who married his niece Milcah and became,…

h5162.g: avenged, Comfort, comfort, comforted, comforter, comforters, comforts, compassion, grieved, minds, pity, regret, regretted, relent, relented, relenting, relents, repent, repented, rid, sorry
h5162.sum: Nâcham is a Hebrew verb that carries two meanings English readers might not expect to share one word: "to comfort" and "to relent." Friends use it when they come to sit with the grieving, as Job's friends did. Prophets use it when God turns back from a disaster He has threatened, as He did for Nineveh. Isaiah uses it when God Himself speaks tender words to an exiled people and promises to rebuild their ruins. Both…

h5184.sum: Nahath is the name of three different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused with one another. The first is a grandson of Esau who became a chief of Edom (Genesis 36:13, 17; 1 Chronicles 1:37). The second is a Kohathite Levite in the ancestry of the prophet Samuel (1 Chronicles 6:26), who appears to be the same man called Toah in 1 Chronicles 6:34 and Tohu in 1 Samuel 1:1. The third is a Levite…

h5221.g: attack, attacked, attacking, attacks, back, beat, beaten, beating, beats, blasted, blows, break, captured, chastened, clapped, condemned, conquer, conquered, damaged, defeat, defeated, defeats, destroy, destroyed, down, drive, drove, entered, executed, indeed, inflicted, inflicting, kill, killed, killing, kills, knock, lengthen, made, manslayer, murder, murdered, murderers, Necho, pin, Pound, punish, received, Shoot, shot, slain, slaughter, slay, slaying, slays, Smitten, stabbed, stricken, Strike, strike, strikes, striking, struck, subdued, surely, thrust, troubled, wounded
h5221.sum: The Hebrew verb nâkâh means to strike: to land a blow, whether with a hand, a rod, a sword, or an army. Depending on the setting, it can describe a beating that wounds, a blow that kills, or a military attack that defeats a whole city. It is one of the most common action words in the Old Testament. It fills the battle accounts of Joshua, Samuel, and Kings. It also governs the laws about violence in Exodus and…

h5248.sum: Nimrod was a descendant of Noah through Ham and Cush. Genesis singles him out as the one who "began to be a mighty one on the earth" (Genesis 10:8). The name is traditionally connected with the Hebrew root marad , "to rebel," and is often explained as "rebel" or "let us rebel." That derivation is a long-standing traditional reading rather than a certain etymology, and Scripture itself never comments on the name's…

h5292.sum: Naarah is the name of two unrelated subjects in the Old Testament: a town on the eastern border of Ephraim's territory (Joshua 16:7) and a woman of the tribe of Judah, one of the two wives of Ashhur, "the father of Tekoa" (1 Chronicles 4:5–6). The name matches the ordinary Hebrew word naʻărâh , meaning "girl" or "young woman." Scripture never explains why a woman or a town carried this name, and nothing in the text…

h5305.sum: Naphish was the eleventh-listed of Ishmael's twelve sons. He was a grandson of Abraham through Hagar, and he became the ancestor of an Arab tribe that bore his name. His name probably means "refreshment" or "refreshed," from a Hebrew root meaning "to breathe" or "to refresh oneself." That meaning is likely but not certain. Naphish appears only three times in Scripture. Two of these are genealogies (Genesis 25:15; 1…

h5315.g: angry, animal, any, anyone, appetite, being, bloodshed, body, breath, corpse, creature, creatures, dead, deadly, desire, discontented, everyone, fancy, greedy, He, he, heart, hearts, hearty, heart’s, her, herself, Him, him, Himself, himself, I, it, itself, life, lifeblood, lives, living, man, Me, me, men, mind, minded, minds, mortally, Myself, myself, neck, ourselves, own, people, perfume, person, persons, pleasure, risk, soul, souls, soul’s, the, themselves, They, thing, those, well-being, Whoever, will, wish, you, yourself, yourselves
h5315.sum: The Hebrew word nephesh describes a living, breathing creature: the whole person as alive, needy, and vulnerable before God. English Bibles translate it "soul," "life," "person," "creature," "heart," "desire," "appetite," and often just "I" or "myself." When God breathed into the dust in Genesis 2:7, "man became a living being," a living nephesh . Hebrew speaks of a person's hunger, longing, fear, love, and very…

h5320.sum: The Naphtuhim were a people descended from Mizraim, the ancestor of Egypt and a son of Ham. They appear only twice in Scripture, in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:13) and in its repetition in Chronicles (1 Chronicles 1:11). Neither passage gives them any action or story, only a name in the family line of Egypt. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is almost certainly an Egyptian phrase carried into Hebrew. Two…

h5434.sum: Seba is first a man and then a people. Genesis names him as the first-listed son of Cush, the son of Ham, and his descendants became a nation remembered in Scripture as distant, wealthy, and impressive. The meaning of the name Seba is unknown. It is a foreign proper name carried over into Hebrew, and no reliable derivation has been established. Seba must not be confused with Sheba, a different name belonging to…

h5454.sum: Sabtah was a son of Cush, a grandson of Ham, and a great-grandson of Noah. His name appears only twice in the Bible, both times in family lists: the Table of Nations in Genesis 10:7 and the matching genealogy in 1 Chronicles 1:9, where the NKJV spells it "Sabta." The meaning of the name is uncertain. It has no clear Hebrew root and probably comes from a non-Hebrew language, perhaps South Arabian. Like many names in…

h5455.sum: Sabteca was the fifth-listed son of Cush, the grandson of Ham, and a great-grandson of Noah. His name appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the list of Cush's sons (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). The NKJV spells it "Sabtechah" in Genesis and "Sabtecha" in Chronicles. The meaning of the name is unknown. Scholars have compared it with the name of a later Cushite ruler of Egypt, Shabataka, but that…

h5513.sum: "Sinite" is the name of an ancient people descended from Canaan, the son of Ham. The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the same short line of a family record: "the Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite" (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15). Scripture tells us nothing about what the Sinites did, whom they fought, or where they worshiped. We know only that they came from Canaan's line and were listed…

h567.sum: The Amorites were one of the peoples living in Canaan before Israel entered the land. Genesis lists them among the descendants of Canaan, and the Old Testament remembers them for their powerful kingdoms, especially those of Sihon and Og east of the Jordan and the five-king alliance Joshua defeated in the south. Sometimes "Amorite" names a specific people or kingdom. At other times it stands for all the inhabitants…

h5677.sum: Eber is best known as the descendant of Shem through whom the Bible traces the line that leads to Abraham. Genesis lists him as the son of Salah (spelled Shelah in Chronicles and Luke), the great-grandson of Shem, and the father of Peleg and Joktan (Genesis 10:21–25; 11:14–17). The name is generally understood to mean "beyond" or "the region beyond." It comes from a Hebrew word family built on a verb meaning "to…

h5762.sum: Avith was a city in the land of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. It appears only twice in Scripture, both times as "his city" of Hadad the son of Bedad, one of the early kings who "reigned in the land of Edom before any king reigned over the children of Israel" (Genesis 36:31, 35; 1 Chronicles 1:46). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Strong's and Smith's Bible Dictionary give the gloss "ruins," and older…

h5780.sum: Uz is the name of three men in the biblical genealogies and of a land east of Israel. The land is by far the most important. The first is a grandson of Shem through Aram (Genesis 10:23; 1 Chronicles 1:17). The second is the firstborn son of Abraham's brother Nahor (Genesis 22:21). The third is a son of Dishan, one of the Horite clan chiefs of Seir, later the territory of Edom (Genesis 36:28; 1 Chronicles 1:42). The…

h583.sum: Enosh was the son of Seth and the grandson of Adam and Eve. He belongs to the third generation of the human story, before the flood. His name is the ordinary Hebrew word for "man," a word that often stresses human frailty and mortality, so it is usually understood as "mortal man." The connection to a root meaning "to be weak" is commonly proposed, though it is less certain than the plain sense "man." Genesis records…

h5858.sum: Ebal is best known as Mount Ebal, the mountain facing Mount Gerizim across the valley at Shechem in the heart of the Promised Land. Moses commanded that when Israel entered Canaan, the curse of God's law would be set on Ebal and the blessing on Gerizim. On Ebal Israel was also to raise great plastered stones inscribed with the law and build an altar of uncut stones for burnt offerings and peace offerings. Joshua…

h5867.sum: Elam is the name of an ancient nation east of Babylon. It is also the name of several Israelites who had no connection to that nation. In Genesis, Elam is a son of Shem and the ancestor of a people who lived beyond the Tigris River in the highlands of what is now southwestern Iran, with Susa (Shushan) as their great city. The name is commonly explained as "highland," associated with the Mesopotamian name for the…

h5891.sum: Ephah is a name carried by three different people in the Old Testament. The best known is Ephah the son of Midian, a grandson of Abraham through Keturah, whose descendants became an Arabian tribe also called Ephah (Genesis 25:4; 1 Chronicles 1:33; Isaiah 60:6). The other two belong to the tribe of Judah: a woman named Ephah who was the concubine of Caleb and bore him three sons (1 Chronicles 2:46), and a man named…

h5902.sum: Iram was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. His name appears only twice in Scripture, as the last entry in the list of Edom's chiefs (Genesis 36:43; 1 Chronicles 1:54). The meaning of the name is probable rather than certain. It seems to come from the Hebrew word for "city" or "town," and lexicons suggest a sense such as "belonging to a city" or "citizen." Genesis lists…

h5907.sum: Achbor is the name of two men in the Old Testament. The first is an Edomite remembered only as the father of Baal-Hanan, one of the early kings of Edom who reigned before Israel had a king (Genesis 36:38–39; 1 Chronicles 1:49). The second, and far more significant, is Achbor the son of Michaiah, a trusted official of King Josiah of Judah. When the Book of the Law was found in the temple, Josiah sent Achbor with four…

h5933.sum: Alvah was one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. He appears only in the list of Edomite clan leaders in Genesis 36:40 and in the Chronicler's repetition of that list, where the name is spelled "Aliah" (1 Chronicles 1:51). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some connect it with a root that suggests height or loftiness (as Hitchcock's dictionary does), while Strong's and…

h5935.sum: Alvan was a son of Shobal, one of the Horite chiefs who lived in Mount Seir before Esau's descendants took over the region. He appears only in the two parallel lists of Seir's family. Genesis 36:23 spells his name Alvan, and 1 Chronicles 1:40 spells it Alian. The difference is often explained as a variation between two similar Hebrew letters. The meaning of the name is uncertain. If it comes from a Hebrew root…

h5978.sum: ʻImmâd is a Hebrew preposition meaning "with," closely related to the much more common ʻim. It carries the ending "me" (ʻimmâdî, "with me"). Context decides what being "with me" means. It can describe a person standing beside the speaker, an action aimed at the speaker for good or harm, something the speaker carries inwardly, or something that belongs to the speaker. With the prefix "from," it marks movement away…

h6002.sum: Amalek is first the name of a grandson of Esau, born to Eliphaz by his concubine Timna (Genesis 36:12), and then, far more often, the name of the desert people descended from him. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Proposed derivations exist, but none is established, and Scripture itself never builds on the name's meaning. The Amalekites lived as nomads and raiders in the Negev and Sinai regions south of Canaan.…

h6034.sum: Anah is the name of two closely related men among the Horites, the people who lived in the mountains of Seir, south of the Dead Sea, before Esau's descendants took the land. The first Anah was a son of Seir the Horite and one of the chiefs of his people (Genesis 36:20, 29). The second was his nephew, a son of Zibeon (Genesis 36:24). This younger Anah became the father of Aholibamah, one of Esau's wives, and of a son…

h6047.sum: The Anamim were an ancient people descended from Mizraim, the Hebrew name for Egypt, who was a son of Ham and a grandson of Noah. Their name appears only twice in the Bible. Both times it comes in the same line of the same genealogy: "Mizraim begot Ludim, Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim" (Genesis 10:13; 1 Chronicles 1:11). Scripture tells us nothing else about them. We do not know where they lived with any certainty,…

h6081.sum: Epher is the name of three different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a son of Midian and a grandson of Abraham through Keturah (Genesis 25:4; 1 Chronicles 1:33). The second is a man of Judah, listed as a son of Ezrah (1 Chronicles 4:17). The third is a clan leader in the half-tribe of Manasseh east of the Jordan, remembered as one of the "mighty men of valor, famous men" (1…

h6186.g: arrange, array, arrayed, charge, compare, compared, direct, directed, equal, established, expert, formation, formed, furnished, handle, joined, Keep, line, Order, order, Ordered, Prepare, prepare, prepared, present, taxed, tend, value, values
h6186.w: Arrange, Set In Order, Array, Prepare
h6186.sum: The Hebrew verb ʻârak means to set things in a row: to arrange, lay out, or put in order. Scripture uses it when Abraham lays the wood on the altar, when priests set out the showbread and tend the lamps, and when armies draw up their battle lines. It is also used for laying out a legal case, preparing a table for a meal, and placing two things side by side to compare them or set a price. The common thread is…

h6208.sum: "Arkite" is the name of an ancient people descended from Canaan, the son of Ham. The Bible uses the word only twice, both times in the same short line of a family record: "the Hivite, the Arkite, and the Sinite" (Genesis 10:17; 1 Chronicles 1:15). The Arkites are linked with the old coastal city of Arqa in what is now northern Lebanon. Ancient records outside the Bible know this city as Irqata. The name places…

h6215.sum: Esau was the firstborn twin son of Isaac and Rebekah, the older brother of Jacob, and the ancestor of the Edomites who settled in the mountain country of Seir. Genesis ties his name to his appearance at birth: "the first came out red. He was like a hairy garment all over; so they called his name Esau" (Genesis 25:25). The name is therefore usually understood as "hairy" or "rough." That meaning rests on the wordplay…

h6258.sum: ʻAttâh is the ordinary Hebrew word for "now." It points to the present moment in contrast to what came before or what lies ahead. Very often, especially in the phrases "and now" or "now therefore," it does more than tell time. It works as a hinge in speech, moving from what has been said to what must happen because of it. A speaker reviews history, states a grievance, or recalls a promise, and then ʻattâh turns the…

h6316.sum: Put is the name of the third son of Ham listed in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:6), and of the African people descended from him. The meaning of the name is unknown. Smith's Bible Dictionary proposes a link to an old word for "bow," but the evidence is thin, and Scripture itself never builds anything on the name. English readers can easily miss Put because the NKJV keeps the name "Put" in Genesis, 1 Chronicles,…

h6370.sum: The Hebrew word pîylegesh means a concubine: a woman joined to a man as a secondary wife. She was publicly recognized as belonging to his household and was expected to be faithful to him, but she held lower standing than a primary wife. Scripture does not set out one uniform package of rights for her across every period, and her children did not necessarily share the chief inheritance, as when Abraham gave gifts to…

h6373.sum: Pinon is one of the chiefs of Edom, the nation descended from Esau, Jacob's twin brother. The name appears only twice, in the closing list of Edomite chiefs in Genesis 36:41 and in the parallel record in 1 Chronicles 1:52. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is widely thought to share a root with Punon, a place in the Arabah where Israel camped during the wilderness years, but no meaning has been firmly…

h6385.sum: The Hebrew verb pâlag means "to divide" or "to split," in the sense of cutting something apart or cutting a channel through it. It appears only four times in the Old Testament, and in each use God is, or is most naturally understood to be, the one who divides. Genesis and 1 Chronicles use it to explain the name of Peleg, "for in his days the earth was divided." The surrounding chapters make it a well-supported…

h6389.sum: Peleg was a descendant of Shem who lived after the Flood. He was the son of Eber, the brother of Joktan, and the father of Reu, and he stands in the family line that runs from Noah to Abraham. His name means "division." Genesis explains why he was given it: "for in his days the earth was divided" (Genesis 10:25). Scripture records no words or deeds of Peleg. What it does preserve is his name, his family, and his…

h6430.sum: Pᵉlishtîy is the Hebrew word for a Philistine, a member of the people who lived along the southern coast of Canaan in cities such as Ashdod, Ashkelon, Ekron, and Gath. The NKJV usually renders it "Philistines" for the nation, "the Philistine" for an individual such as Goliath, and occasionally "Philistia" for their land. The word names a people. It does not mean "enemy" or "wicked." Still, no nation pressed harder…

h6435.sum: Pên introduces an outcome that someone wants to prevent. It usually follows a command, a warning, a decision, or a prayer, and then names the danger that the command, warning, decision, or prayer is meant to avoid. The NKJV most often renders it "lest." After words like "beware" or "swear," it often becomes a simple "not," and in Genesis 31:31 it appears as "Perhaps," voicing Jacob's fear. Wherever it appears, pên…

h6440.sum: The Hebrew word pânîym means "face." Because the face is where a person is recognized, where feelings show, and where one person meets another, the word naturally came to mean "presence." To be before someone's face was to be in their company and under their gaze. The same word also became Hebrew's most common way of saying "before," "in front of," "from," and even "because of." It can describe the surface of the…

h6464.sum: Pau was a royal city in Edom, the land of Esau's descendants south and southeast of the Dead Sea. Scripture names it only as the city of Hadar, the eighth and last-listed of the Edomite kings in Genesis 36. First Chronicles 1:50 repeats the record, calling the king Hadad and the city Pai. No one knows exactly what the name means. It is often linked to a Hebrew root meaning "to cry out" or "to bleat," but that…

h6625.sum: Pathrusim is the name of a people. It refers to the descendants of Mizraim (Egypt) who settled in Pathros, the southern stretch of the Nile valley usually called Upper Egypt. The word appears only twice in the Bible. Both times it sits in a list of nations descended from Ham: Genesis 10:14 and its parallel in 1 Chronicles 1:12. Neither verse tells a story about the Pathrusim. They are named, placed in their family…

h6649.sum: Zibeon was a Horite chief who lived in Mount Seir, the rugged highlands south of the Dead Sea that later became the land of Edom. He was one of the sons of Seir the Horite, the clan leaders who held the land before Esau's descendants took it over (Genesis 36:20, 29). His family joined Esau's when Esau married Aholibamah, a descendant of Zibeon usually traced through his son Anah (Genesis 36:2, 14, 24–25), though…

h6664.g: altogether, cause, earth, honest, just, Justice, justice, right, Righteous, righteous, righteously, RIGHTEOUSNESS, Righteousness, righteousness, rightful, unrighteousness
h6664.sum: Tsedeq is the Hebrew word for what is right, meaning what measures up to a true standard. Its roots in Scripture are concrete. The law uses it for honest scales and full weights in the marketplace and for fair verdicts in court. From there the word rises to describe God Himself: His throne rests on righteousness, His Word is righteous through and through, and His judgments never tilt toward the powerful or the bribe.

h6721.sum: Sidon was an ancient Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean coast, north of Israel. Genesis also gives the name to a person: "Canaan begot Sidon his firstborn" (Genesis 10:15). The firstborn of Canaan and the old coastal city stand at the head of the Canaanite peoples. The name most likely means "hunting" or "fishing." It is usually traced to a Hebrew root meaning to hunt or catch, which suits a seafaring town,…

h6757.sum: Tsalmâveth is the Hebrew Bible's word for the deepest darkness a person can know. The NKJV renders it "shadow of death" every time it appears. Its range covers the grave, a killing wilderness, the black interior of a mine, the gloom over a grieving face, and the darkness of people imprisoned by their own rebellion. It names more than the moment of dying. It describes the darkness in which death feels near,…

h6786.sum: "Zemarite" is the name of an ancient people descended from Canaan, the son of Ham. It appears only twice in Scripture, both times in the same short line of a genealogy: "the Arvadite, the Zemarite, and the Hamathite" (Genesis 10:18; 1 Chronicles 1:16). The word carries no abstract meaning. It names a real tribe, usually linked with the coastal city of Sumur (Simyra) in what is now coastal Syria, near the far…

h6825.sum: Zepho was a grandson of Esau, the son of Eliphaz, Esau's firstborn by Adah (Genesis 36:10–11). Zepho's own mother is not identified. He appears only in the family records of Edom. Genesis lists him among Eliphaz's sons and then names him "Chief Zepho," one of the clan leaders who governed Esau's descendants in the land of Seir (Genesis 36:15). First Chronicles repeats his name in its survey of the nations…

h687.sum: Ezer was a Horite chief in the land of Seir, the rugged mountain country south of the Dead Sea that later became Edom. He was one of the seven sons of Seir the Horite, and he headed a clan whose sons are named as Bilhan, Zaavan, and Akan (called Jaakan in Chronicles). His name, ʼEtser, comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to store up" or "lay up," so it is usually understood to mean "treasure" or "store." He should not…

h6887.g: adversaries, afflict, afflicted, Afflicting, affliction, besiege, besieges, Bind, binds, bound, danger, distress, distressed, enemies, enemy, Harass, harass, harassed, hindered, mended, narrow, oppressed, oppresses, pangs, rival, small, trouble, up, wrapped
h6887.sum: The Hebrew verb tsârar means to bind, wrap, cramp, or hem in. It can describe something physical: kneading bowls bundled in clothing, a stone tied into a sling, or a place too small to live in. It can also describe a person pressed in by circumstances until no way out remains. That person is in "distress" or "trouble." And it can describe someone who presses others in, the "enemy" or "adversary" who harasses and…

h6929.sum: Kedemah is the last-named of the twelve sons of Ishmael, Abraham's son by Hagar. His name appears only twice in Scripture, both times in a list: once in the family record of Ishmael (Genesis 25:15) and again in Chronicles' retelling of the same line (1 Chronicles 1:31). His name is traditionally understood to mean "eastward" or "toward the east." It is related to the Hebrew word for "east," which can also carry the…

h6938.sum: Kedar was the second-listed son of Ishmael and a grandson of Abraham through Hagar (Genesis 25:13; 1 Chronicles 1:29). His descendants became a powerful nomadic Arabian tribe east of Israel. They were known for their archers, their large flocks, and their black tents, and the Bible later uses the name for the people and their desert region. The name is generally traced to a Hebrew root meaning "to be dark" or…

h6989.sum: Keturah was a woman Abraham married. Genesis introduces her after the narrative of Sarah's death and Isaac's marriage, and on the traditional sequential reading the marriage came late in Abraham's life. Genesis introduces her in one plain line: "Abraham again took a wife, and her name was Keturah" (Genesis 25:1). Her name is widely understood to come from the Hebrew root associated with incense and the rising smoke…

h7018.sum: Kenan was one of the early patriarchs before the flood. He was the son of Enosh, the father of Mahalalel, and the fourth generation from Adam through Seth. Readers of the NKJV will find him under the spelling "Cainan" in Genesis 5:9–14 and 1 Chronicles 1:2, and again in Luke's genealogy of Jesus (Luke 3:37). The meaning of his name is uncertain. Scholars have connected it with a Hebrew root meaning "to acquire" or…

h7073.sum: Kenaz is the name of several men in the Old Testament. The first is an Edomite chief, a grandson of Esau through his son Eliphaz (Genesis 36:11, 15). The most significant is a man of Judah remembered as the father of Othniel, the first judge of Israel (Joshua 15:17; Judges 3:9). A third is a later descendant of Caleb, the son of Elah (1 Chronicles 4:15). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Strong's suggests a…

h7141.sum: Korah is the name of several men in the Old Testament. Edom's family records mention one or two Korahs (the references may concern the same chief or clan), and one appears in the genealogy of Judah. The Korah who matters most is the Levite, son of Izhar and grandson of Kohath, who led a rebellion against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness (Numbers 16). The name is traditionally understood to mean "baldness," and some…

h721.sum: "Arvadite" is a Hebrew name for a people: the Arvadites, a Canaanite clan who lived in Arvad, an island city off the northern coast of Phoenicia (modern Arwad, Syria). The word appears only twice in the Bible, in Genesis 10:18 and 1 Chronicles 1:16. Both verses list the Arvadites among the descendants of Canaan, the son of Ham, in the "Table of Nations," the record of how the families of the earth spread out after…

h7218.g: bands, beginning, beginnings, beheaded, capitals, captains, census, chief, chiefs, choicest, companies, company, count, divisions, ends, entirety, every, excellent, first, forehead, fork, front, full, hair, head, heads, high, highest, honor, it, its, lead, leader, leaders, master, men, mountaintop, mountaintops, of, over, primal, quality, released, riverheads, Rosh, sum, things, top, topmost, tops, value
h7218.sum: The Hebrew word rôʼsh means "head." Most often it is the physical head of a person or animal, but Hebrew speakers naturally extended the word to whatever stands first or highest. It can be the top of a mountain or tower, the beginning of a year or a river, the chief of a family or army, the finest of the spices, or the full sum of a count. Wherever it appears, it marks the place of first rank.

h7257.g: down, lay, lie, lies, lying, rest, settle, sheepfolds, sitting
h7257.sum: The Hebrew verb râbats describes an animal folding its legs beneath it and settling to the ground. Sheep lie down in a pasture, a donkey sinks under a heavy load, a mother bird sits on her eggs, and a lion stretches out in its den. The posture is the same each time. Context decides whether it means safety, exhaustion, protection, menace, or royal ease. When the verb takes a causative form, it means "to make lie…

h7291.g: after, chase, chased, flight, Follow, follow, follows, hunts, past, persecute, persecuted, persecutors, Pursue, pursue, pursued, pursuer, pursuers, pursues, pursuing, pursuit
h7291.sum: Râdaph is the Hebrew verb for running after something in order to catch it. It describes armies chasing a beaten enemy, a hunter tracking game, a hostile man hounding the innocent, and a person who gives himself wholeheartedly to a goal. Most often the word sounds dangerous. Pharaoh's chariots pursue Israel to the sea, Saul hunts David through the wilderness, and the psalmists cry out against those who persecute…

h7310.sum: The Hebrew noun rᵉvâyâh describes abundance as a state of being filled to the point of overflow. It belongs to a word family that speaks of drinking deeply and having one's thirst fully quenched. The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the Psalms, and both times God is the One who brings it about. In Psalm 23:5 David says, "My cup runs over," while the Lord spreads a table for him in front of his…

h7344.sum: Rehoboth is the name of three different places in Genesis and 1 Chronicles. The name means "broad places," "open spaces," or "streets," and comes from a Hebrew root meaning to be wide or roomy. The first Rehoboth is Rehoboth Ir, a city in Assyria listed among the early building projects connected with Nimrod (Genesis 10:11). The second is a well in the southern wilderness that Isaac named after two bitter disputes…

h7384.sum: Riphath was the second-listed son of Gomer, a grandson of Japheth, and a great-grandson of Noah. His name appears only in the family lists of the nations that spread across the earth after the flood (Genesis 10:3; 1 Chronicles 1:6). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Riphath is an ancient tribal name, and no explanation of it has been established. Scripture records no deeds, speeches, or later history for him. He…

h7451.g: adversities, adversity, affliction, afflictions, bad, burdensome, calamity, catastrophe, cruel, deadly, deeply, defect, destruction, Disaster, disaster, displease, displeased, displeasing, distress, distressing, doom, Evil, evil, evils, exceedingly, grave, great, harm, harmful, Harsh, heavy, hurt, ill, miser, misery, misfortune, not, nothing, painful, raving, ruin, sad, serious, severe, suffer, terrible, things, trouble, troubles, ugly, wicked, wickedly, wickedness, wild, woe, worst, wronged
h7451.sum: The Hebrew word raʻ is the Old Testament's ordinary word for what is bad. It is the opposite of "good," and it covers a wide range. It can describe moral wickedness: the evil a person plans, speaks, or does against God and neighbor. It can also describe what is harmful or painful without any sin implied, such as sickly cattle, a heavy task, a sad face, a dangerous animal, or a national disaster. English translations…

h7454.sum: The Hebrew word rêaʻ means a thought: what a person has in mind, including intentions and purposes. It is one of the rarest words in the Old Testament. It appears only twice, and both times in Psalm 139. In verse 2 David uses it for his own mind: "You understand my thought afar off." Fifteen verses later he uses it for God's mind: "How precious also are Your thoughts to me, O God!"

h7466.sum: Reu was the son of Peleg and the father of Serug, a descendant of Shem who lived in the generations after the Flood, in the era commonly associated with the scattering at Babel. His name probably means "friend" or "companion." It is generally connected with the Hebrew word for a friend or neighbor, though the derivation is not certain. Scripture records almost nothing about his life. Genesis 11:18–21 gives his…

h7467.sum: Reuel is a Hebrew personal name generally understood to mean "friend of God," formed from a word for "friend" or "companion" joined to El , "God." Four different men carry it in Scripture, and they should not be confused with one another. The first is a son of Esau by Basemath, Ishmael's daughter, who became the father of several clan chiefs in Edom (Genesis 36). The second is the priest of Midian who took in Moses…

h7473.g: devours, eat, eaten, fed, Feed, feed, feeding, feeds, forage, graze, herdsmen, keep, keeper, keeping, pasture, pastured, rulers, Shepherd, shepherd, shepherded, shepherdess, Shepherds, shepherds, shepherd’s, tending, waste
h7473.sum: The Hebrew word rôʻîy means a shepherd. It belongs to the family of the verb râʻâh (H7462), "to pasture, feed," the Bible's ordinary shepherding vocabulary. That family describes sheep and cattle grazing, the shepherd who leads them to pasture, and the person who does that work: Abel the keeper of sheep, Rachel the shepherdess, the boy David out with the flock. Israel's kings and leaders were called shepherds…

h7484.sum: Raamah was a son of Cush and a grandson of Ham, named in the Table of Nations after the Flood (Genesis 10:7; 1 Chronicles 1:9). His name later stands for the people and region descended from him, an Arabian trading nation that Ezekiel lists among the merchants who enriched the city of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:22). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some connect it to a Hebrew root associated with thunder or trembling,…

h753.g: Forever, forever, high, Length, length, long
h753.sum: The Hebrew noun ʼôrek means "length." Most often it gives the long measurement of something God told His people to build: Noah's ark, the tabernacle and its furniture, Solomon's temple, and the temple Ezekiel saw in vision. Again and again Scripture records "the length shall be..." because God was not vague about the places where He would save, meet, and dwell with His people. Holiness came with exact dimensions.

h758.g: Aram, Mesopotamia, Syria, Syrian, Syrians, Syria’s
h758.sum: Aram is the Hebrew name for the Arameans and their homeland, the cluster of kingdoms north and northeast of Israel centered on Damascus. The NKJV usually translates it "Syria." The same name also belongs to three individuals: a son of Shem in the table of nations, a grandson of Abraham's brother Nahor, and a little-known man of the tribe of Asher. The name is traditionally understood to mean "high" or "exalted,"…

h7586.sum: Saul was the first king of Israel, a son of Kish from the tribe of Benjamin, whose reign marks the troubled passage from the days of the judges to the house of David. His name means "asked for." The Hebrew is drawn from the ordinary verb "to ask," and the meaning is woven into the story itself. Israel asked for a king like all the nations (1 Samuel 8), and God gave them a man whose very name said "asked for." Paul…

h7614.sum: Sheba is the name most closely associated with a wealthy trading people of southern Arabia, the Sabeans, though not every biblical Sheba group can simply be identified with that southern kingdom. Scripture traces the name through three separate genealogical lines: a descendant of Ham through Cush, a descendant of Shem through Joktan, and a grandson of Abraham through Keturah. The meaning of the name itself is…

h7626.g: correction, rod, Scepter, scepter, spears, staff, tribe, tribes
h7626.sum: The Hebrew word shêbeṭ names a stick or rod of wood. What it means in a given passage depends on whose hand holds it. A king holds it as a scepter , a shepherd as a rod to guard and count his flock, and a father or master as a rod of correction. A warrior can carry it as a club or a dart. Most often in the Old Testament it names a tribe of Israel, a household gathered under the authority its leader's staff…

h765.sum: Aran was a Horite, one of the early inhabitants of Mount Seir, the rugged highland south of the Dead Sea that later became the land of Edom. Scripture names him only twice, both times in the same short line of genealogy: "The sons of Dishan were Uz and Aran" (1 Chronicles 1:42; compare Genesis 36:28). His father Dishan was one of the sons of Seir the Horite, which makes Aran a grandson of Seir. The meaning of his…

h7725.sum: The Hebrew verb shûwb means to turn back or return. In daily life it describes a traveler heading home, a dove flying back to the ark, or a lender handing back a borrowed cloak. It can also mean to bring something back: to restore stolen property, recover captives, or give back an answer. From these ordinary uses the Old Testament draws one of its central pictures of life with God. Sin is a turning away from Him,…

h7732.sum: Shobal is the name of at least two different men in the Old Testament, and they should not be confused. The first is a Horite chief, a son of Seir, whose people lived in the hill country of Seir before Esau's descendants took it over (Genesis 36:20–29; 1 Chronicles 1:38–40). The second is a man of the tribe of Judah, a son of Hur and a descendant of Hezron's son Caleb. Chronicles calls him "Shobal the father of…

h7744.sum: Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah, Abraham's wife, also called a concubine. Genesis introduces her after Sarah's death; the traditional reading places the marriage then, though the text does not settle its timing. He is named last among her six sons in Genesis 25:2 and again in 1 Chronicles 1:32. His name is probably related to a Hebrew verb meaning "to sink down" or "to bow down," which suggests a sense such as…

h775.sum: Arphaxad (also spelled Arpachshad) was a son of Shem and a grandson of Noah. He was born "two years after the flood" (Genesis 11:10), so he belongs to the first generation of the world that came out of the ark. The meaning of his name is uncertain. It may not be Hebrew in origin. Its last letters resemble Kesed , the root behind the Hebrew name for the Chaldeans, so some scholars have suggested a link to Chaldea or…

h776.g: common, countries, country, countryside, distance, Earth, earth, field, floor, ground, Land, land, lands, lowland, nations, shore, territories, wasteland, wilderness, world
h776.sum: ʼErets is the ordinary Hebrew word for the earth beneath our feet. It can mean the whole created world, a particular country such as Egypt or Canaan, or simply the ground where someone bows or falls. It is one of the most common nouns in the Old Testament. It opens the Bible, where God created the heavens and the earth, and it carries the story through Abraham's call, Israel's inheritance, exile, and the promise of…

h790.sum: Eshban was a Horite, one of the sons of Dishon. His family belonged to the people who lived in the mountains of Seir, south of the Dead Sea, before the descendants of Esau took the land. He appears only twice in Scripture, in Genesis 36:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:41, both times as a name in a family list. The meaning of his name is uncertain. Older proposals link it to Hebrew words for "fire" or "understanding," but…

h7974.sum: Shelah was a son of Arphaxad and grandson of Shem. He lived in the generations after the Flood and was the father of Eber. His name, Hebrew Shelach (שֶׁלַח), comes from a root meaning "to send." Its exact meaning as a personal name is uncertain. The noun can mean "a missile" or "weapon," something sent out, and it can also mean "a shoot" or "sprout," something a plant sends forth. Genesis records nothing he did…

h7979.sum: The Hebrew word shulchân means "table." It names an ordinary piece of furniture where people ate, but Scripture sets it in some of the Bible's most moving scenes. In the tabernacle, God commanded a gold-covered table to stand in the Holy Place, holding bread "before Me always." In David's palace, a lame grandson of Saul named Mephibosheth was given a permanent seat at the king's table. In the psalms, God prepares a…
