h802.sum: Ishshâh is the ordinary Hebrew word for a woman. Hebrew has no separate word for "wife," so the same word names both a woman and a married woman. "His woman" means "his wife," and context decides which English word fits. The word runs from the creation of Eve to Malachi's teaching about marriage. It names the matriarchs and the women protected in Israel's laws. It names mothers, widows, prophetesses, queens, and the…

h8026.sum: Sheleph is one of the thirteen sons of Joktan named in the Table of Nations (Genesis 10:26) and again in the Chronicler's opening genealogy (1 Chronicles 1:20). He belongs to the family of Shem through Eber, and his descendants were among the Joktanite peoples whose homeland Genesis describes as stretching "from Mesha as you go toward Sephar, the mountain of the east" (Genesis 10:30). His name is commonly connected…

h8034.g: byword, fame, famous, infamous, Name, name, named, names, name’s, place, renown, report, there, vile
h8034.sum: The Hebrew word shêm means "name." It is the ordinary word for what a person, place, or thing is called, from the rivers of Eden to the sons of Jacob. In Hebrew usage, though, a name goes further than a label. It stands for how someone is known: their reputation and their remembered identity. Men of great reputation are "men of renown," a ruined reputation is a "bad name," and a man's name surviving in Israel means…

h8035.sum: Shem was the son of Noah, the brother of Ham and Japheth, and one of the eight people who came through the Flood alive. His name is spelled exactly like the ordinary Hebrew word for "name," and it carries the sense of renown or reputation. That simple meaning becomes surprisingly important in Genesis. The builders of Babel tried to "make a name" for themselves and were scattered. The very next section of Genesis…

h804.sum: Asshur is the Hebrew name for Assyria. Scripture uses the name for a man, a land, and an empire: Asshur the son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), the land along the upper Tigris that bore his name, and the empire that rose from that land to dominate the ancient Near East. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Older lexical tradition proposes "a step" or "successful," but neither meaning is firmly established. What is clear…

h8048.sum: Shammah is a name shared by several different men in the Old Testament, and the first task is keeping them apart. One is an Edomite chief, a grandson of Esau (Genesis 36:13, 17; 1 Chronicles 1:37). Another is the third son of Jesse of Bethlehem, an older brother of David, who passed before Samuel and heard the prophet say, "Neither has the LORD chosen this one" (1 Samuel 16:9). A third, Shammah the son of Agee the…

h8072.sum: Samlah was an early king of Edom, the nation descended from Esau. He is the fifth ruler named in the Edomite king list of Genesis 36, and the same list is repeated in 1 Chronicles 1. His name most likely means "garment" or "mantle." It matches the ordinary Hebrew word for a cloak or wrapper, though Scripture never comments on why he bore it. The Bible tells us only three things about him: he came from a place called…

h8081.g: anointing, fat, fatness, fruitful, Oil, oil, Ointment, ointment, ointments, olive, perfumes, pieces, verdant
h8081.sum: The Hebrew word shemen means oil, above all the oil pressed from olives. In Israel it was part of ordinary life. Women baked with it, families burned it in their lamps, people rubbed it on their skin and faces, and healers applied it to wounds. It was also the oil God chose for His holiest purposes. Poured on Aaron's head, it set him apart as priest. Poured from Samuel's horn, it marked David as king, and Scripture…

h813.sum: Ashkenaz appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, but those few verses carry the name from the first generations after the flood to the fall of Babylon. In Genesis 10:3 and 1 Chronicles 1:6, Ashkenaz is a son of Gomer, a grandson of Japheth, and a great-grandson of Noah. In Jeremiah 51:27 the name has become a kingdom, one of the northern powers God summons against Babylon alongside Ararat and Minni. The…

h8147.g: another, Both, both, couple, double, double-edged, pair, parties, second, sixty-two, twelfth, Twelve, twelve, twenty, Twice, twice, Two, two
h8147.sum: Shᵉnayim is the ordinary Hebrew word for "two." It counts people, animals, objects, and years, and it is often translated "both," "pair," or "couple." In combination with other words it also produces "twelve," "twelfth," "second," "twice," "double," and larger numbers such as "sixty-two." Most of its uses are plain counting. Two sons, two pillars, and two loaves need no hidden meaning.

h8165.sum: Seir is the rugged mountain country south of the Dead Sea that God gave to Esau and his descendants, the Edomites. The same Hebrew name also belongs to Seir the Horite, an ancestor of the people who lived there before Esau. It also names a separate Mount Seir on Judah's northern border. The name is commonly understood to mean "hairy" or "shaggy," probably describing rough, brush-covered hill country. Hebrew readers…

h8195.sum: Shepho was a Horite of Mount Seir, the rugged highland south of the Dead Sea that later became Edom. He was the son of the chief Shobal and a grandson of Seir the Horite. Genesis does not list Shepho himself among the chiefs. Genesis spells his name Shepho (Genesis 36:23), and 1 Chronicles spells it Shephi (1 Chronicles 1:40). The meaning of the name is uncertain. Lexicons link it to a Hebrew root meaning "to sweep…

h8286.sum: Serug was a descendant of Shem who lived in the generations between the flood and Abraham. He was the son of Reu, the father of Nahor, the grandfather of Terah, and the great-grandfather of Abram. His name most likely comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to intertwine," and some interpreters render it "branch" or "shoot." That meaning is a probable derivation rather than a settled one. Genesis records only a few facts…

h8352.sum: Seth was the third named son of Adam and Eve, born after Cain murdered Abel. Genesis itself explains his name. Eve named him Seth because, she said, "God has appointed another seed for me instead of Abel, whom Cain killed" (Genesis 4:25). The name is tied to the Hebrew verb meaning "to put, set, or appoint," so Seth carries the sense of "appointed" or "set in place." His birth answered the first great crisis after…

h8422.sum: Tubal is the fifth listed son of Japheth and a grandson of Noah. His name also became the name of a people who descended from him. The meaning of the name is uncertain. Some connect it with a root meaning "to bring" or "brought," but the Bible gives no explanation of the name, and no derivation is settled. Tubal appears only eight times in Scripture. Genesis and 1 Chronicles list him among the founders of the…

h8425.sum: Togarmah is named only four times in Scripture, but the name covers a long distance. He first appears in the Table of Nations as the third listed son of Gomer and a great-grandson of Noah through Japheth (Genesis 10:3; 1 Chronicles 1:6). In Ezekiel the name has become a people, "the house of Togarmah," a northern nation that traded horses, steeds, and mules with the merchant city of Tyre (Ezekiel 27:14). Ezekiel…

h8435.g: birth, genealogies, genealogy, generations, history, records
h8435.sum: Tôwlᵉdâh is the Hebrew word for the "generations" that come from a person or a starting point: the descendants, family lines, and unfolding history that follow from an origin. The NKJV translates it "genealogy," "genealogies," "generations," "history," "records," and once "birth." It gives Genesis its framework. Again and again the book pauses to say, "This is the genealogy of…" or "This is the history of…", and…

h8454.g: guidance, judgment, plans, prudence, success, Wisdom, wisdom
h8454.sum: Tûwshîyâh is a Hebrew word for wisdom that works. The NKJV translates it as "sound wisdom," "success," "prudence," "plans," "judgment," and "guidance." The range of translations makes sense once we see the idea behind them. This word describes good sense and the ability to carry it through to a good result. It is wisdom with substance, the kind that holds up when life puts weight on it.

h8478.g: as, below, beneath, flat, foot, for, Instead, instead, is, Mine, place, places, sake, spot, to, Under, under, underneath, where, Whereas, Why, with
h8478.sum: Tachath is a common Hebrew word of position. At its simplest it means "under," "beneath," or "below": the waters under the firmament, a traveler resting under a tree, enemies brought low under a king's feet. From that idea of standing in a spot it also comes to mean "in place of" or "instead of," the place one thing takes when another is removed or exchanged. A son reigns in his father's place, and a ram is offered…

h8485.sum: Tema was the ninth listed son of Ishmael. His name also became the name of the tribe descended from him and of their settlement, a well-watered oasis in northwestern Arabia on the caravan routes that ran between southern Arabia and the lands to the north. The meaning of the name is uncertain. It is sometimes linked to a root meaning "desert" or to the idea of "south," but neither derivation is established. Tema…

h8487.sum: Teman is first a man and then a land. He was the first listed son of Eliphaz and a grandson of Esau, and he became one of the chiefs of Edom (Genesis 36:11, 15). His name came to belong to an important region of Edom, so prominent that the prophets often used "Teman" to stand for the whole Edomite nation. The name means "south." It is related to the Hebrew word for "right hand," because a person facing the sunrise…

h8489.sum: "Temanite" names a person who comes from Teman, a leading region or town of Edom, the land settled by the descendants of Esau. The word describes origin, so its meaning is simply "one from Teman." The place name Teman is generally connected with the Hebrew word for "right hand," and from that with "south," because a person facing east to get his bearings has the south on his right. That derivation is widely held but…

h8494.sum: Tiras is the last of the seven sons of Japheth listed in the Table of Nations. He is a grandson of Noah, and he stands as the ancestor of a people who settled somewhere in the wider world after the Flood (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). The meaning of his name is uncertain. h85.sum: Abraham is the patriarch whom God called out of a family that worshiped other gods. God made him the father of Israel and, through his Seed, the father of all who believe. He was born Abram, a name usually understood to mean "exalted father." When he was ninety-nine, God renamed him Abraham, and Scripture explains the new name itself: "for I have made you a father of many nations" (Genesis 17:5). The Hebrew sound of…

h8549.sum: The Hebrew word tâmîym describes something whole, sound and complete, with nothing missing or damaged. It most often describes the animals Israel brought to the LORD, which had to be "without blemish," such as the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:5) and the daily burnt offerings. h8555.sum: Timna is a name from the family records of Edom in Genesis 36 and 1 Chronicles 1. It most clearly belongs to a Horite woman, the sister of Lotan and daughter of Seir, the original people of the mountain country south of the Dead Sea. h8646.sum: Terah is best known as the father of Abram (later Abraham), Nahor, and Haran. He was a descendant of Shem who lived in Ur of the Chaldeans, led his household out toward Canaan, stopped at Haran, and died there at two hundred and five years old (Genesis 11:24–32). h8659.sum: Tarshish is best known in the Bible as a distant, wealthy seaport or region at the far edge of the ancient world, famous for its silver and metals and for the large ocean-going "ships of Tarshish" named after it. h87.sum: Abram is the son of Terah from Ur of the Chaldeans. God called him to leave his homeland and go to a land He would show him, and he became the man through whom God promised to bless "all the families of the earth" (Genesis 12:3). h911.sum: Bedad was an Edomite, a descendant of Esau's people, and Scripture remembers him only as the father of Hadad, one of the early kings of Edom. His name appears twice, in parallel records: "Hadad the son of Bedad, who attacked Midian in the field of Moab, reigned in his place" (Genesis 36:35; 1 Chronicles 1:46).
